# Feeling curve, peak, signature move, fingerprint gate

Condensed from `upstream/scroll-craft/.../references/feel.md` and
`uniqueness.md` §§3–4. Design the feeling before the acts: a device chosen
before the emotion is a device looking for a reason.

## The feeling curve

One line per act in `BRIEF.md`, written **before a single act exists**: the
emotion, then what on screen causes it. The emotion is the constraint; the
device name only ever appears in the cause column, second.

```
1  Recognition   their own kitchen counter at 7am, shot at eye height
2  Fatigue       the two containers, the mess, held still while copy names it
3  Delight       a wipe, and the whole frame is one cold can, condensation running
4  Trust         macro texture at a scale the eye cannot get in a shop
5  Appetite      the flavours travelling sideways, each one landing whole
6  Resolve       everything stops, one can, one line, one place to buy it
```

Two adjacent acts with the same feeling means one is filler — cut it or
change what it does. The curve outranks the Step 1 journey beats: beats say
what the visitor learns, the curve says what they feel while learning it, and
where they disagree the curve wins.

## The peak

People remember one peak and the ending; the middle compresses into a general
impression. So every build engineers **one** deliberate peak, named in
`BRIEF.md` as the sentence a visitor would say to a friend ("the screen went
black and then the whole ocean lit up under me" — a moment, not "the hero is
impressive"). The peak gets, at the expense of every other act:

| It gets | Because |
|---|---|
| The asset budget | Best generated frames or the only real footage go here |
| The silence before it | A quiet act or empty viewport, so the change has something to be a change from |
| The most scroll room | Largest `data-sc-span` on the page, `dwell` tuned to settle exactly there |

A page with three peaks has none — demote the losers (shorter span, plainer
device). The close must resolve, not trail off: the divider collapses, the
world lands somewhere, the type quiets — never a fade to an empty stage.

## The tell-someone test

Complete, before building: *"it's the site where ___."* "It has a scrub
video" is a device name — no hook. "You drag the letters of the logo apart
and they snap back perfectly" is an experience — that's a hook. The blank has
to be something that happened **to the visitor**. This sentence usually
contains the signature move; if the tell-someone sentence and the signature
move point at different moments, one of them is decoration.

## The signature move

One bespoke interaction that exists on this build alone — coded in the page
off `--sc-p` or a page-authored `data-sc-*`, never a parameter on a kit
device, never in any prior build. The engine stays untouched.

**What counts** (upstream examples, not a menu to pick from): scroll-as-
playhead over a persistent trace rail; a wordmark the pointer pulls apart and
snaps back exactly; a line drawing whose `stroke-dashoffset` is driven from
`--sc-p`; a running receipt that accumulates real figures; one control that
regrades the whole page at once (time-of-day, temperature, load).

**What does not count**: a recoloured/resized spotlight; `data-sc-tilt` turned
up; a different easing on kinetic lines; more cards in a rail; a third
`scrub` act; anything the engine already does under a project class name.
Test: describe the move to someone who has seen the other builds — if they
can't tell it apart from something the kit already does, it isn't one.

## Being in it, not watching it

Upstream `feel.md` § 4. *"A film plays whether you are there or not. The
difference between a viewer and a participant is whether the page acknowledges
that somebody specific is here: how fast they are moving, where their pointer
is, whether they stopped."*

Five techniques, in the kit's own vocabulary:

- **Pointer parallax that moves the world, not a card.** `data-sc-spotlight`
  publishes `--sc-mx` / `--sc-my`. Drive a *background layer's* transform off
  them instead of a highlight, and the environment shifts as the visitor
  moves, slightly, the way a real space does when you lean.
- **Dwell-triggered detail.** Hold still on an act and something further
  arrives — a caption, a second line, a small annotation. Reward for stopping.
  Mechanically: **read `--sc-p` staying constant across a few frames**, in the
  page's own JS, and reveal something that was **never needed for
  comprehension**.
- **Scroll velocity shaping intensity.** Fast scrolling raises grain, blur,
  chromatic offset, ground saturation; slow scrolling settles it. *"The page
  feels like it is being driven rather than played back, and it costs one
  derived custom property."*
- **The page addressing "you" at one moment that lands.** Not throughout,
  which is just copywriting. **One line**, at the emotional turn, in second
  person, when the visitor is already implicated. *"It works because it is the
  only time."*
- **A trace of where they have been.** Anything that accumulates as they
  travel, so arriving at the end means having a record rather than reaching a
  footer.

**Embodiment is seasoning. One or two per page.** *"A page that reacts to
everything feels haunted, not alive: the visitor stops reading and starts
poking, which is the opposite of what any of this is for."* Pick the one that
serves the peak and leave the rest.

These are gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` — a pointer-capability
query, which stands.
Upstream also turns them off under reduced motion — **that half utgår, F-011**.
The rule that does survive is upstream's own:
*"a technique that only exists on desktop cannot be the thing that carries the
page's meaning."*

## Pacing as emotion

Upstream `feel.md` § 5. *"Scroll distance is emotional time. It is the only
clock this medium has, and it is fully under your control, which makes it the
cheapest emotional instrument in the kit and the one most often left at
default."*

| Pacing | Reads as | Built with |
|---|---|---|
| Short acts, hard cuts | Adrenaline, pulse, impatience | Acts under 1.4 vh, no `pin`, `dwell` at 0 |
| A long pin | Held breath, pressure, attention | `data-sc-span` 3+, overlapping cues, one idea |
| An empty viewport before a reveal | Silence before the drop | A ground-only act, no cue until the next one |
| A slow settle mid-act | The shot landing | `data-sc-dwell` 0.35–0.6, cue peak on the settle |
| A fast cue with a long plateau | Confidence, arrival | `data-sc-cue="0.1 0.9 0.08 0.4"` |
| A slow ramp in | Hesitation, dawning | Long `rampIn` — **once per page**, it is close to feeling broken |

Four rules follow:

- **Silence must be authored, not left over.** *"An empty screen you meant
  reads as anticipation. An empty screen you did not mean reads as a page that
  failed to load, and the harness reports both as dead scroll."* If the empty
  viewport before the peak is deliberate, **say so in `BRIEF.md`** so the
  verification pass can tell it from dead scroll. This is the sentence that
  keeps `scroll_verify.py`'s `blankBands` check from being either useless or a
  false alarm.
- **Give the peak room.** The peak act has the largest span on the page by a
  visible margin. *"If every act is 2.2 vh, the page has no shape, whatever
  the curve in BRIEF.md says."*
- **Compress the administrative parts.** Specs, logistics, FAQ, credentials
  are information, not experience — flow sections at short stagger, never
  pinned acts with dwell. Spending scroll on them spends the visitor's
  patience on the part they will not remember.
- **A continuous world is the exception to pacing variety.** All of the above
  is about a page of *acts*. A worldflight is one camera move, and *"a camera
  that changes speed between legs reads as broken rather than as
  expressive."* There, hold one pace and let the peak carry the shape by being
  the single long leg — [`pace.md`](pace.md).

The total-length budget stays **8–14 viewport-heights**. Pacing is how that
budget is spent, not permission to spend more: *"a page that needs 20 vh to
land its curve has too many acts, not too little room."*

## The fingerprint gate

Registry: `VAULT/wiki/projects/_index/design-fingerprints.md`, per-vault,
starting from whatever rows already exist — not repeating **yourself** across
builds, not a universal constraint. **Six dimensions**, recorded per row:

| # | Dimension | What it records |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grammar | Which of `grammars.md`, or a named new one |
| 2 | Nav treatment | What the chrome is and what it's for |
| 3 | Hero device | What the first screen does |
| 4 | Act-sequence shape | Device order, act count, total viewport-heights |
| 5 | Close pattern | How the last screen behaves, what the CTA sits in |
| 6 | Signature move | The one bespoke interaction, in a phrase |

**The gate: a new build must differ from EVERY existing row on at least 4 of
the 6** — four against each row individually, not averaged across the table.
Dimension 6 is free (unique by definition), so the gate really asks for 3
more out of the remaining 5 against each row. If the plan fails, **change
the plan, not the log** — rewriting a row to fit is what makes it worthless.

**Row format** — one row per shipped build, all six dimensions plus a world
note and the path: `| Build | Grammar | Nav | Hero device | Act-sequence
shape | Close pattern | Signature move | Register | World / palette | Path |`

**Rows are append-only.** From upstream `templates/FINGERPRINTS.md`:

> *"A build that has been superseded stays in the table, because the space it
> occupies is still occupied."*

A replaced, retired or rejected build keeps its row. The registry does not
record what is live; it records what surface has already been taken, and a
surface stays taken whether or not the build that claimed it is still up.
Deleting a row silently frees a shape for reuse, which is the same failure as
editing one to make room — *"never edit a row to make room for it. If a
planned build fails, change the plan."*

**Fill every column.** A row with blanks cannot be scored 4-of-6 against, so
it weakens the gate for every build after it.

**Keep a "what is taken" list beside the table.** Add a bullet whenever a
build claims something a later build should avoid reusing: a grammar, a nav
treatment, a close pattern, a signature move, an act-count-and-length band.
*"The shared columns are what the next build inherits as a constraint, so
writing them down is the whole point."*

After shipping, append the row and say what it shares with prior rows — the
shared columns are exactly what the *next* build has to avoid.

1	# Motion
2	
3	Most AI-generated motion is scattered — hover lifts on every card, fade-in on every scroll, bouncing icons. Quiet it. One orchestrated moment beats ten small ones.
4	
5	> For per-interaction recipes (button press, focus, modal, toast, optimistic update, command palette, drag handle, etc.), see [`microinteractions.md`](microinteractions.md). This file is the *language* of motion; that file is the *vocabulary*.
6	>
7	> For scroll-driven acts — the device kit, pace, the feeling curve — see [`scroll/`](scroll/README.md). The 300 ms UI budget below does not govern them; see § Scroll-linked motion.
8	>
9	> For the *stepping* and *dropped-frames* faults behind "hackigt och billigt", see [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md) and [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md).
10	
11	## The motion thesis
12	
13	Write it before implementation, in `BRIEF.md`, in four lines. Ported from impeccable `animate.md` § Set the motion thesis:
14	
15	- **Focal moment** — the one sequence or interaction that deserves authorship, if any.
16	- **Continuity** — the state, layout, or navigation changes that need explaining.
17	- **Feedback** — the controls and outcomes that need acknowledgment.
18	- **Budget** — which effects may be expensive, and how often they run.
19	
20	> "The focal moment must come from this product and surface concept. A generic fade-and-rise, hover lift, parallax layer, or scroll reveal is not a thesis."
21	
22	Find the job first: inspect the existing motion language, states, target devices and performance budget, and animate **only** where motion would acknowledge an action, make a state change or spatial relationship legible, preserve continuity through a layout change, direct attention at a meaningful moment, or embody the selected world. "Do not animate a static area merely because it exists."
23	
24	**One sentence per animation** (taste-skill § 5). Every animation that ships names, in the brief, what it communicates. An animation with no sentence is decoration and gets cut — that is the same test as impeccable's "decoration without purpose is animation debt", made countable.
25	
26	**Rejected candidates are part of the output.** `find-animation-opportunities` requires the rejected list; so does this file. A motion thesis that lists only what was built cannot be reviewed.
27	
28	## The build sequence
29	
30	Seven decisions, in this order, from emil `animate` § The Build Sequence. Steps 1 and 2 gate everything: **do not reach for a curve before you know whether it animates at all.**
31	
32	1. **Should this animate at all?** — the frequency gate below.
33	2. **What is the purpose?** — name it in one word: feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation, delight. "Can't name it? Don't build it."
34	3. **Pick the tool — cheapest that works.** CSS transition → `@starting-style` → CSS animation → WAAPI → a motion library. Walk down, stop at the first that fits. CSS animations run off the main thread and beat JS under load; use CSS for predetermined motion, JS for dynamic and interruptible motion.
35	4. **Pick the properties** — § Material by meaning.
36	5. **Easing and duration, or a spring** — § Easings, § Durations.
37	6. **Interruption and exit** — § Interruption and exit.
38	7. **Pointer gating** — `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` ships with the animation, not as a follow-up. (Upstream's step 7 pairs this with a `prefers-reduced-motion` branch. That half does not port: **F-011**.)
39	
40	| Frequency | Decision |
41	|---|---|
42	| 100+ times/day (keyboard shortcuts, command palette toggle) | **No animation. Ever.** Stop here |
43	| Tens of times/day (hover effects, list navigation) | Near-imperceptible only — fast and subtle, or nothing |
44	| Occasional (modals, drawers, toasts) | Standard animation |
45	| Rare / first-time (onboarding, success, a landing page's one set-piece) | The delight budget lives here |
46	
47	"Keyboard-initiated actions are a disqualifier, not a judgment call." A Persuade surface is seen once by each visitor, which is why it gets the authored moment an Operate surface must not have.
48	
49	**No approximated values.** Every curve, duration and spring config comes from the tables in this file. Never invent `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)` because it looks familiar. And **extend the page's existing tokens, don't fork them** — adding a parallel motion scale beside `--ease-*` / `--dur-*` is a defect.
50	
51	## Principles
52	
53	- **`transform` and `opacity` are the floor, not the ceiling.** They are GPU-composited and skip layout, so they carry the routine work. The hard rule is the narrower one, in impeccable `motion-design.md`'s own words: *"The hard rule is not 'transform and opacity only.' The hard rule is: avoid animating layout-driving properties casually (`width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, margins), keep expensive effects bounded to small or isolated areas, and verify in-browser that the result is smooth on the target viewports."* See § Material by meaning. **This supersedes the earlier absolute "only `transform` and `opacity`"** — that line banned `clip-path`, `filter` and masks, which are the chain's own reveal and depth vocabulary (scroll-craft `reveal`, kinetic masks, the blur crossfade). The layout-property ban is untouched and absolute.
54	- **Duration is four buckets.** Micro (100–150ms), minor (150–300ms), major (300–500ms), and one authored focal entrance (500–800ms) per page. Exits are ~75% of the enter.
55	- **Easing is exponential ease-out.** Elements coming in slow down into place. Elements leaving accelerate away.
56	- **Motion serves perception.** If you can't explain what a transition communicates, cut it.
57	- **Never animate text colour.** Photosensitive risk (designpowers `motion-choreography` § What NOT to Animate). Cross-fade the element or swap the node; do not run a colour transition on a run of text.
58	- ~~**Reduced motion is non-optional.**~~ **F-011 (2026-09-07):** superseded — rörelsen spelar alltid i det här designsystemet; ingen `prefers-reduced-motion`-gren byggs och ingen granskare flaggar att den saknas. Funktionell rörelse (progress, spinners, skeletons) är oförändrad.
59	
60	## Easings
61	
62	Use these three. Name them as tokens.
63	
64	```css
65	:root {
66	  --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);        /* elements entering */
67	  --ease-in:  cubic-bezier(0.7,  0, 0.84, 0);       /* elements leaving  */
68	  --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1);    /* state toggles     */
69	}
70	```
71	
72	`ease`, `ease-in-out` (default), `cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1)` — these are the browser defaults and they read as uncrafted.
73	
74	Three named alternates, from emil `emil-design-eng` § 3 and `animate` § 5. Use them when the curve above is not the right shape; do not hand-roll a fourth.
75	
76	```css
77	:root {
78	  --ease-out-strong:    cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1);    /* strong ease-out for UI      */
79	  --ease-in-out-strong: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1);   /* strong on-screen movement   */
80	  --ease-drawer:        cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1);    /* iOS-like drawer (Ionic)     */
81	}
82	```
83	
84	And the exponential ramp, from impeccable `motion-design.md` § Easing, when a micro-interaction wants friction rather than a curve name:
85	
86	```css
87	--ease-out-quart: cubic-bezier(0.25, 1, 0.5, 1);   /* smooth, refined — recommended default */
88	--ease-out-quint: cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);  /* slightly more dramatic                */
89	--ease-out-expo:  cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);   /* snappy, confident                     */
90	```
91	
92	**Two conflicts, resolved.**
93	
94	- **Which `--ease-out`?** Upstream emil names `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; this file's `--ease-out` is `cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)` (identical to impeccable's `--ease-out-expo`). **This file's value wins**, because the shipped builds, `house-physics.md` and `microinteractions.md` already carry it and a second `--ease-out` is exactly the forked token set step 3 forbids. Emil's rule is *"built-in CSS easings are too weak"*, not *"this cubic-bezier specifically"* — a strong custom curve satisfies it, and `review-animations` standard 3 asks for a custom curve, not for that one. Emil's value stays available as `--ease-out-strong`.
95	- **`ease` on hover.** Emil's decision tree sends hover/colour changes to built-in `ease`. **The ban in § Bans wins.** A hover that only changes colour reads identically under `--ease-out` at ≤150 ms, and keeping one token set is worth more than the last few percent of that curve. Nothing on this page uses the browser default.
96	
97	**`ease-in` is for exits only.** Elements leaving the screen accelerate away (impeccable `motion-design.md` § Easing: *ease-in → "Elements leaving"*). Never `ease-in` on anything entering, on anything moving on screen, or on anything the user is waiting for — *"it starts slow, which makes the interface feel sluggish and unresponsive… the exact moment the user is watching most closely."* This is a **known, deliberate divergence** from `review-animations` standard 3 and its escalation trigger "`ease-in` on any UI interaction": that trigger reads a bare `ease-in` as a defect, and here a bare `ease-in` on an exit is correct. State it in the review so the reviewer does not re-flag it; every other use of `ease-in` remains a block.
98	
99	## Durations
100	
101	```css
102	:root {
103	  --dur-micro: 120ms;   /* button press, toggle tick, color shift  */
104	  --dur-short: 220ms;   /* hover lift, tooltip, menu open          */
105	  --dur-long:  420ms;   /* modal, drawer, accordion, page reveal   */
106	  --dur-focal: 640ms;   /* the one authored focal entrance         */
107	}
108	```
109	
110	Exits use roughly 75% of the enter:
111	
112	```css
113	.menu.is-open  { transition: transform var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out); }
114	.menu.is-close { transition: transform calc(var(--dur-short) * 0.75) var(--ease-in); }
115	```
116	
117	**The band each token sits in** — impeccable `motion-design.md` § Duration (the 100/300/500 rule) and `animate.md` § Timing and easing, which agree row for row:
118	
119	| Duration | Use |
120	|---|---|
121	| 100–150 ms | Immediate feedback — button press, toggle, colour change |
122	| 150–300 ms | Routine state change — menu open, tooltip, hover state |
123	| 300–500 ms | Layout change — accordion, modal, drawer, view transition |
124	| 500–800 ms | A **deliberately authored** focal entrance: page load, hero reveal. One per page |
125	
126	**Per element**, when the band is too coarse (emil `emil-design-eng` § 4):
127	
128	| Element | Duration |
129	|---|---|
130	| Button press feedback | 100–160 ms |
131	| Tooltips, small popovers | 125–200 ms |
132	| Dropdowns, selects | 150–250 ms |
133	| Modals, drawers | 200–500 ms |
134	| Marketing / explanatory | Can be longer |
135	
136	**UI animations stay under 300 ms.** *"A 180 ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400 ms one."* Anything slower on a UI element needs a stated reason or it is a finding. `--dur-focal` is that stated reason, used once.
137	
138	**Reach for a spring instead** when the motion is a drag with momentum, an element that should feel alive, a gesture the user can interrupt or reverse, or decorative pointer tracking:
139	
140	```js
141	{ type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }            // Apple-style, easier to reason about
142	{ type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }  // traditional physics, more control
143	```
144	
145	Keep bounce at 0.1–0.3 and avoid it in most UI. Apple's own defaults, from `apple-design` § 4: **damping 1.0** (critically damped, no overshoot) everywhere by default; **damping ~0.8 only when the gesture itself carried momentum** — a flick, a throw, a drag release. *"Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong; overshoot on a card you flicked feels right."* Response 0.3–0.4 s; response is not duration — a spring has no fixed duration, its settle time emerges from the parameters.
146	
147	## Material by meaning
148	
149	Impeccable `animate.md` § Choose material by meaning. Pick the property for what the transition *communicates*, not for what is cheapest to type:
150	
151	| Communicates | Material |
152	|---|---|
153	| Continuity and relationship | Shared-element motion, FLIP-style transforms, View Transitions, deliberate spatial movement |
154	| Focus and depth | Bounded `blur`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter`, light and shadow change |
155	| Reveal and composition | Masks, `clip-path`, cropping, controlled occlusion |
156	| Material and energy | Colour, gradient position, texture, distortion, shader work where the world and runtime support it |
157	| State and feedback | The smallest change that makes cause and result unmistakable |
158	| Expanding layout | `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr` or a FLIP transform — never `height` directly |
159	
160	> "Do not stack techniques for spectacle. One strong material idea, carried through the focal sequence and quiet supporting states, is usually enough."
161	
162	Three constraints that come with the wider palette:
163	
164	- **Bound the expensive ones.** Blur, filter, backdrop, canvas and shader work stay in small or isolated regions. Keep blur under 20 px — heavy blur is expensive, especially in Safari.
165	- **`clip-path` is the sanctioned fourth property** beside `transform`, `opacity` and `filter`. `height` is tolerated only for accordions, where there is no transform equivalent.
166	- **Measure, don't assume.** *"Verify in-browser that the result is smooth on the target viewports"* — `transform` does not mean fast, and a bounded blur that measures smooth is allowed even though it is not composited. `scripts/motion_probe.py` is the instrument; see [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md).
167	
168	Property picks that are not negotiable (emil `animate` § 4):
169	
170	- **Never `scale(0)`.** Start from `scale(0.9–0.97)` + `opacity: 0`. Nothing in the real world appears from nothing.
171	- **Percentages in `translate()`** are relative to the element's own size — `translateY(100%)` moves it by its own height whatever the content. Prefer them to hardcoded pixels.
172	- **Never drive a child's transform from a CSS custom property on the parent.** It recalculates styles for every child — a style-recalc storm, and one of `review-animations`' flag-on-sight triggers. Set `transform` on the element itself. (The scroll engine's `--sc-p` is the deliberate exception: it is read by `calc()` in the child's *own* rule, not written per frame onto a parent that has children to invalidate.)
173	- **In a motion library, write the full transform string.** `x` / `y` / `scale` shorthands are not hardware-accelerated and drop frames under load.
174	
175	## Page-load orchestration
176	
177	One sequence on page load. Stagger by DOM index using a CSS custom property, not by JS.
178	
179	```html
180	<section style="--i: 0">…</section>
181	<section style="--i: 1">…</section>
182	<section style="--i: 2">…</section>
183	```
184	
185	```css
186	.reveal {
187	  opacity: 0;
188	  transform: translateY(8px);
189	  animation: reveal var(--dur-long) var(--ease-out) forwards;
190	  animation-delay: calc(var(--i, 0) * 60ms);
191	}
192	@keyframes reveal {
193	  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
194	}
195	```
196	
197	Cap total stagger at ~500ms. Beyond that the page feels slow to settle.
198	
199	**Stagger has three limits, not one:**
200	
201	- **30–80 ms between siblings.** Longer feels slow. (designpowers `motion-choreography` names 50–80 ms; that sits inside this range and is a fine default for a group of cards.)
202	- **Maximum 5 items staggered — the rest appear together.** A ten-item stagger is a queue, not choreography.
203	- **Follow reading order**, and let the sequence reveal hierarchy: the item that matters arrives first.
204	
205	Sibling stagger is appropriate *when a list appears as a list*. "Never reinterpret every scrolled section as a staggered list", and never stagger a routine interaction — a row hover, a keystroke, a repeated tab change.
206	
207	**Blur is the third stagger channel**, beside opacity and translate (interfaces `better-ui/enter-exit.md` § Enter animations). Combine `opacity`, `filter: blur()` and `translateY` for a staged entrance; the blur is what makes the arrival read as focus pulling in rather than as a card sliding:
208	
209	```css
210	.stagger-item {
211	  opacity: 0;
212	  transform: translateY(12px);
213	  filter: blur(4px);
214	  animation: fade-in-up 400ms var(--ease-out) forwards;
215	  animation-delay: calc(var(--i, 0) * 60ms);
216	}
217	@keyframes fade-in-up {
218	  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; filter: blur(0); }
219	}
220	```
221	
222	Split a large container into semantic groups (title, description, buttons) at ~100 ms between groups; for a display title, splitting into words at ~80 ms is the finer grain. Exits carry the same three channels in reverse and stay softer — a small fixed `translateY(-12px)` plus `blur(4px)` at ~150 ms, because "the user's focus is moving to the next thing, so do not fight for it."
223	
224	## Interruption and exit
225	
226	Emil `animate` § 6, interfaces `better-ui/animations.md` § Interruptible animations, `apple-design` § 3. Apple calls interruptibility *"the single most important principle"*, and the chain agrees: an animation the reader cannot grab mid-flight is what reads as the page ignoring them.
227	
228	| | CSS transition | CSS keyframes |
229	|---|---|---|
230	| Behaviour | Interpolates toward the latest state | Runs on a fixed timeline |
231	| Interruptible | **Yes — retargets mid-animation** | **No — restarts from the beginning** |
232	| Use for | Interactive state changes: hover, toggle, open/close | Staged sequences that run once: entrances, loaders |
233	
234	- **Transitions, not keyframes, for anything triggered rapidly** — toasts, toggles, anything a user can fire twice in a second. Keyframes on a rapidly-triggered element is an automatic block. "Clicking again mid-animation smoothly reverses"; the keyframe version "snaps or restarts, feels broken."
235	- **Always animate from the *presentation* value, never the target value.** On interrupt, read the element's live on-screen transform and start the new animation from there. *"Starting from the logical/target value causes a visible jump."* This is the single most common cause of a flip or drawer that reads as cheap on the second interaction.
236	- **Springs for gestures**, because they carry velocity through an interruption and animate from the current value by default. Never lock out input during a transition.
237	- **Blend velocity at a reversal, don't hard-cut it.** Swapping one animation for another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity — a "brick wall". Decompose 2D motion into independent X and Y springs; one spring on a 2D distance desyncs when the two axes have different velocities.
238	- **Exit the way it entered.** A toast that slides in from the bottom leaves through the bottom. Symmetric paths are what make swipe-to-dismiss feel obvious.
239	- **Asymmetric timing where the user is deciding.** Slow on the deliberate phase (a hold-to-confirm press: 2 s linear), snappy on the system response (release: 200 ms ease-out). Symmetric timing on a press-and-release is a finding.
240	- **No `animation-fill-mode: forwards` or delays that block interaction** on a panel the user can re-trigger — the transition should simply respond to the new state.
241	
242	## Origin and anchoring
243	
244	Refero `motion.md` § Transform Origin and emil `animate` § 4. Getting the origin wrong is read as "hackigt och billigt" long before anyone can name it: the element scales from the wrong place, so it appears to come from nowhere.
245	
246	**Set `transform-origin` explicitly on every scale or rotate.** The defaults:
247	
248	| Element | Origin |
249	|---|---|
250	| Modal | `center` — **exempt**, it is not anchored to a trigger |
251	| Dropdown / popover / menu | The trigger: `top left` or `top right` (`var(--transform-origin)` in Base UI) |
252	| Tooltip | The edge closest to the trigger |
253	| Button press | `center` |
254	
255	`transform-origin: center` on a trigger-anchored popover is an automatic block.
256	
257	**SVG needs `transform-box: fill-box`.** A transform on an SVG child resolves against the viewBox, not the element, so `transform-origin: center` lands somewhere else entirely:
258	
259	```css
260	/* wrong: resolves against the viewBox */
261	svg path { transform: rotate(45deg); }
262	
263	/* right */
264	svg g.icon-wrapper {
265	  transform-box: fill-box;
266	  transform-origin: center;
267	  transform: rotate(45deg);
268	}
269	```
270	
271	This is a **build rule, not a review note**, on any page whose art is inline SVG — which is most illustrated and typographic-poster work here. A whole page of inline-SVG marks rotating around the wrong point is one missing declaration, and it is F-012-class: the motion runs and looks wrong.
272	
273	## Scroll-linked motion
274	
275	**"UI under 300 ms" does not apply to scroll-driven acts.** The 300 ms budget above governs *UI elements* — a dropdown, a tooltip, a modal, anything the user triggered and is now waiting on. A scroll-driven act is **paced by the hand**: the reader sets its speed, there is no wait to shorten, and its duration is a distance in viewport-heights rather than a number of milliseconds. A 1.4-second reveal or a scrubbed card flip inside a declared act is therefore **correct, not a finding**, and `review-animations` must be told so before it reads the diff. What still applies inside an act: the easing bans, the origin rules, interruptibility, the property list, and the pace bar in [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md).
276	
277	On an ordinary (non-act) page:
278	
279	- Use IntersectionObserver, **never** an unstructured `scroll` handler. Unobserve after a once-only reveal fires.
280	- Use it only for *reveal once* effects. Content that re-hides on the way back up is a defect, not an effect.
281	- **The permitted scroll-listener form**, when a page genuinely drives a value from scroll position: a **passive** listener that only records a number, **one** rAF loop that does the writing, a **deadband** below which nothing is written, and **no layout reads inside the handler**. That is what the vendored engine does; a handler that reads `getBoundingClientRect()` per event is the banned form. Never touch React (or any framework) state from a rAF loop.
282	- ~~Every scroll-triggered motion must have a reduced-motion fallback.~~ **F-011 (2026-09-07):** utgår; scrollstyrd rörelse har en väg, och den verifieras.
283	
284	**The scroll-reveal recipe** (emil `animate/RECIPES.md` § Scroll reveal). Marketing surfaces only — "don't do this to functional UI a user visits daily":
285	
286	```css
287	.reveal {
288	  clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);
289	  transition: clip-path 600ms var(--ease-in-out);
290	}
291	.reveal[data-visible] { clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0); }
292	```
293	
294	Trigger once with IntersectionObserver at a `-100px` root margin. *"Fire it once — re-animating on every scroll-by is an interface fighting its reader."* `clip-path` is relative to the **border box, not the ink**: on type set below `line-height: 1` the wipe shears ascenders and descenders off and every figure renders as a bar. Put `data-*` reveal attributes on a wrapper, or give the element room.
295	
296	**Masking a crossfade that won't settle** (`RECIPES.md`). When two states overlap visibly and no amount of easing or duration tuning fixes it, blur the seam:
297	
298	```css
299	.content { transition: filter 200ms var(--ease-out), opacity 200ms var(--ease-out); }
300	.content.transitioning { filter: blur(2px); opacity: 0.7; }
301	```
302	
303	*"Without blur the eye reads two distinct objects swapping. Blur blends them into one perceived transformation."* (Upstream writes both transitions with the built-in `ease`; retimed to `--ease-out` here so the recipe does not ship a § Bans violation. The blur value and the 200 ms are upstream's.)
304	
305	**Parallax, reconciled with § Bans.** The ban below stands for *casual* parallax — a background image drifting on an ordinary page because it was easy. Parallax as a **declared device inside a scroll grammar** is sanctioned, and only under the rate discipline and layer rules in [`scroll/devices.md`](scroll/devices.md) § 6: the rate is hundreds of pixels of total travel, adjacent planes differ by 10–30%, copy rides at 1×, never body copy on a moving layer, and never a `transition: transform` on a parallaxed element.
306	
307	## Choreography per section (GSAP + Lenis)
308	
309	**Every section gets one row in a choreography table before code.** Element →
310	motion → trigger → duration/ease → reduced-motion state. The motion is chosen from
311	the element itself — headline, image, list, card — not picked off a menu of
312	available effects. Template: `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3f/RORELSE-SPEC.md`
313	(anti-slop-design repo) — a per-section spec written this way, opening with the
314	grip in one sentence, is what separated a 30%-image-area composition from a
315	4.3%-image-area document on the same brief (see [`inspo-mcp.md`](inspo-mcp.md)).
316	
317	**Reading rule: every headline stands fully visible, unclipped and still for
318	≥ 40 vh of scroll.** Motion plays only before and after that window — never during
319	it. Cropping a word is only allowed where the glyphs lose something that does not
320	carry the reading (descenders, one side of an overhanging letter) — **never the
321	baseline.** A first impression the reader can't hold still on long enough to read
322	is not a reveal, it's a miss.
323	
324	**Fail toward visible, with self-completion.** Any reveal or interaction that gates
325	content completes itself: the contact card flips itself at section progress 0.7 whether
326	or not the reader ever touches it; jumping to an anchor or scrolling to the page's
327	max shows the final state, not a mid-animation one. Check template:
328	`max_scroll_residual_check()` in `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3f/verify_motion.py` — after
329	`lenis.scrollTo('bottom', {immediate:true})`, every element must be at its resting
330	transform, not partway through a rise or sweep.
331	
332	**State switches crossfade, never snap.** A tab, a case choice, a step change —
333	opacity/transform tweens, interruptible — never a hard class-toggle snap. Stacked
334	steps share one grid cell (`grid-area: 1/1`) so the swap costs no layout shift
335	(V3d's `.cs` pattern).
336	
337	**Iframes and embeds load before the interaction that reveals them, and never
338	navigate during a transition.** A same-origin document still loading inside a
339	just-revealed or just-pinned element is a race the browser loses visibly.
340	
341	**An image-area floor is never met by enlarging the same image.** Screenshots used
342	as thumbnails are shot fresh at 2× and shown zoomed out — not the same low-res
343	capture blown up to fill the slot.
344	
345	## State transitions
346	
347	- Button hover / active: micro duration, `--ease-out`, `transform: translateY(-1px)` on hover, `translateY(0)` on active. Never a `box-shadow` transition on hover on a dark background (glow effect).
348	- Menu / tooltip / dropdown: short duration, `--ease-out` on open, `--ease-in` on close. Use the popover API or `inert` to manage focus.
349	- Modal: long duration, scale-in (0.96 → 1) + opacity crossfade. Backdrop fades in at the same duration.
350	- Accordion: animate `grid-template-rows: 0fr` → `grid-template-rows: 1fr` (not `height`). With `--ease-in-out`.
351	
352	## Felt state to property
353	
354	From designer-skills `interfaces-that-feel`. Use it when a page is technically correct and lands cold — the translation runs in four steps, and the point is that "premium" is a *behaviour*, not a value you can pick:
355	
356	1. **Name the felt state** — what the person is actually experiencing at this moment. Not the task. Waiting. Recovering from an error. Arriving somewhere.
357	2. **Find the physical analogue** — what in the physical world has that quality. "Soft surfaces absorb impact. A held breath before exhaling. The slow release of a door."
358	3. **Extract the behavioural property** — weight, resistance, speed, recovery arc, rhythm.
359	4. **Apply it to a layer** — easing curve, delay, duration, spacing, colour temperature, copy tone.
360	
361	The translation, in this file's terms:
362	
363	| Felt state | Reads as | Built with |
364	|---|---|---|
365	| Heavy, consequential | Weight and momentum | Longer duration, **larger travel distance**, ease-out with a long tail |
366	| Light, incidental | Quick and unremarkable | Shorter duration, **smaller travel distance**, `--dur-micro` |
367	| Confident, arriving | Deceleration into place | `--ease-out-quart` / `--ease-out-expo`, a plateau at the end |
368	| Snappy, responsive | Stiff spring | High stiffness, damping 1.0, no overshoot |
369	| Playful, forgiving | Loose spring | Lower damping, bounce 0.1–0.3, **only after a gesture with momentum** |
370	
371	Two timing rules that come with it: **information weight** — heavy news arrives slowly, good news can be instant; and **recovery space** — after an error, give 300–600 ms before the next prompt rather than rushing the recovery. Linear is mechanical; keep it off anything that touches human feeling (progress bars and ticking loaders excepted).
372	
373	## Perceived performance
374	
375	Impeccable `motion-design.md` § Perceived Performance. *"Nobody cares how fast your site is, just how fast it feels."*
376	
377	- **The 80 ms threshold.** The brain buffers sensory input for roughly 80 ms to synchronise perception, so anything under 80 ms reads as instant and simultaneous. That is the target for micro-interactions, and it is why `--dur-micro` sits where it does rather than lower.
378	- **Preemptive start.** Begin the transition immediately while loading, rather than after. The user perceives work happening.
379	- **Early completion.** Show content progressively — progressive images, streaming markup — instead of waiting for everything.
380	- **Optimistic UI.** Update the interface immediately and handle failure gracefully. For low-stakes actions only; never for payments or destructive operations.
381	- **Easing changes perceived duration.** Ease-out feels satisfying for entrances; ease-in toward the *end* of a task compresses perceived time, because the peak-end effect weights the final moments heavily.
382	- **A fast spinner makes a load feel faster**, at an identical load time. Instant tooltips after the first one make a whole toolbar feel faster.
383	- **Caution.** Too-fast responses can decrease perceived value — users distrust an instant result for a complex operation. Sometimes a brief delay signals that real work happened.
384	
385	## Reduced motion — utgår (F-011)
386	
387	```css
388	/* F-011 (2026-09-07): reduced-motion-blocket utgår — rörelsen spelar alltid, aldrig en preferensgrind. */
389	```
390	
391	Functional motion (progress bars, loading spinners, skeletons) is unchanged — it runs at its normal speed. ("Just slower" was the reduced-motion branch's wording and went with it; F-011 leaves functional motion alone rather than degrading it.)
392	
393	**What F-011 dropped, and from where.** Every upstream package this file draws on ships a `prefers-reduced-motion` half; **none of it lands here (F-011)**. Motion plays unconditionally, no build reads a browser or OS preference to switch it off, and no reviewer flags its absence. Listed so nobody re-imports one of them believing it was an oversight:
394	
395	| Source | Block dropped | Why |
396	|---|---|---|
397	| emil `review-animations` § The Ten Non-Negotiable Standards | **Standard 8's first half** — "`prefers-reduced-motion` is honored (gentler, not zero)" | F-011. Standard 8's **second half — hover gating behind `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` — is kept** and is in the build sequence, step 7 |
398	| emil `animate` § 7 + § Never Ship | The `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` branch, `useReducedMotion()`, and the "Missing `prefers-reduced-motion`" row | F-011. The pointer-gating half of both is kept |
399	| emil `review-animations` escalation triggers | "Missing `prefers-reduced-motion` handling on movement" | F-011. "Ungated `:hover` motion" is kept |
400	| impeccable `motion-design.md` § Reduced Motion | The whole section, including the `animation-duration: 0.01ms !important` reset and the "vestibular disorders affect ~35% of adults over 40" framing, plus the § Avoid line "Ignoring `prefers-reduced-motion`" | F-011, and F-011 records that this is a **deliberate, informed** trade against exactly that population — not an oversight to be quietly corrected |
401	| designpowers `motion-choreography` § Reduced Motion | The standard/reduced alternatives table and **"Every animation must have a reduced-motion alternative. No exceptions."** | F-011. Its § What NOT to Animate (text colour, layout properties, decorative loops) is kept |
402	| taste-skill § 5 / § 6.B | `useReducedMotion()` gating in the scroll skeletons; "Reduced Motion (mandatory)" | F-011 |
403	| interfaces `better-ui/animations.md` § Motion restraint | The clause "Users with reduced motion enabled…" inside the two-channel rule | F-011 for the clause only. **The rule survives**: motion is never the only feedback channel — a state change an animation communicates stays visible when the animation does not run, for anyone who simply blinked |
404	| scroll-craft `devices.md` §§ 1, 3, 9 · `feel.md` § 4 · `worldflight.md` § 8 | Every "under reduced motion…" branch: lerp rate 1.0, the `pan` scroll-region floor, pointer-device disabling, embodiment gating, the hard-rules exception | F-011. The `pan` **reachability** requirement survives on its own terms — see [`scroll/devices.md`](scroll/devices.md) |
405	
406	WCAG 2.3.1 (the three-flashes-per-second limit) is untouched. It is a safety limit, not a preference.
407	
408	## Never Ship
409	
410	Self-check before finishing. Each row is an automatic block in `review-animations` (emil `animate` § Never Ship, twelve of thirteen rows — the missing `prefers-reduced-motion` row is dropped per F-011, see § Reduced motion).
411	
412	| Never | Instead |
413	|---|---|
414	| `transition: all` | Name the exact properties |
415	| `transform: scale(0)` entrance | `scale(0.95)` + `opacity: 0` |
416	| `ease-in` on anything entering or on screen | `ease-out` or a strong custom curve (exits excepted — see § Easings) |
417	| Built-in `ease-out` on a deliberate animation | `--ease-out`, or `--ease-out-strong` |
418	| Animation on a keyboard shortcut or a 100+/day action | No animation |
419	| UI duration over 300 ms with no reason | 150–250 ms (`--dur-focal`, once, is the stated reason; a scroll act is exempt) |
420	| `transform-origin: center` on a trigger-anchored popover | The trigger's corner (modals exempt) |
421	| Keyframes on toasts, toggles, rapidly-triggered elements | CSS transitions |
422	| Animating `width` / `height` / `margin` / `padding` / `top` / `left` | `transform` / `opacity` (accordion: `grid-template-rows`) |
423	| Motion-library `x` / `y` / `scale` props under load | The full `transform` string |
424	| Ungated `:hover` motion | `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` |
425	| Everything entering at once | 30–80 ms stagger, max 5 items |
426	
427	**When feel can't be settled from code, say so and check it** rather than guessing at a value (emil `animate` § Output, `review-animations` § Debugging). Four instruments: play it at **2–5× duration** or in the DevTools animation inspector; step it **frame by frame** to catch timing drift between coordinated properties; test gestures on a **real device**, not headless; and **look again the next day** — imperfections invisible during development surface with fresh eyes. Report findings as a **Before / After / Why** table.
428	
429	## Bans
430	
431	- `ease` (browser default, mediocre).
432	- `linear` on anything except progress bars and ticking loaders.
433	- Bounce / elastic / overshoot on UI elements. Dated; signals "template".
434	- Animating `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, `padding`.
435	- `will-change` set preemptively across a whole class. Only on the element, only while it's animating. (The vendored `scrollcraft.css` sets it preemptively on seven class-level selectors and so breaks this ban. **The engine is never edited** — the deviation is documented in [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md) and cleared at runtime by the shim, not by touching the engine.)
436	- Casual parallax — see § Scroll-linked motion for the declared-device exception.
437	- `transition: transform` on any element that a scroll or pointer loop writes every frame. The transition eases each per-frame write over its own duration, and on a phone the element reads as lagging a full second behind the thumb. Parallaxed and magnetised elements transition **opacity only**.
438	- Custom cursors.
439	- Text-colour transitions (photosensitive risk).
440	- A CSS custom property on a parent used to drive children's transforms (style-recalc storm).
441	- ~~Scroll-driven animations without a reduced-motion fallback.~~ **F-011 (2026-09-07):** inte längre ett fel.
442	- Infinite loops (other than functional loaders) — they pull the eye and never let go.
443

# Motion

Most AI-generated motion is scattered — hover lifts on every card, fade-in on every scroll, bouncing icons. Quiet it. One orchestrated moment beats ten small ones.

> For per-interaction recipes (button press, focus, modal, toast, optimistic update, command palette, drag handle, etc.), see [`microinteractions.md`](microinteractions.md). This file is the *language* of motion; that file is the *vocabulary*.
>
> For scroll-driven acts — the device kit, pace, the feeling curve — see [`scroll/`](scroll/README.md). The 300 ms UI budget below does not govern them; see § Scroll-linked motion.
>
> For the *stepping* and *dropped-frames* faults behind "hackigt och billigt", see [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md) and [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md).

## The motion thesis

Write it before implementation, in `BRIEF.md`, in four lines. Ported from impeccable `animate.md` § Set the motion thesis:

- **Focal moment** — the one sequence or interaction that deserves authorship, if any.
- **Continuity** — the state, layout, or navigation changes that need explaining.
- **Feedback** — the controls and outcomes that need acknowledgment.
- **Budget** — which effects may be expensive, and how often they run.

> "The focal moment must come from this product and surface concept. A generic fade-and-rise, hover lift, parallax layer, or scroll reveal is not a thesis."

Find the job first: inspect the existing motion language, states, target devices and performance budget, and animate **only** where motion would acknowledge an action, make a state change or spatial relationship legible, preserve continuity through a layout change, direct attention at a meaningful moment, or embody the selected world. "Do not animate a static area merely because it exists."

**One sentence per animation** (taste-skill § 5). Every animation that ships names, in the brief, what it communicates. An animation with no sentence is decoration and gets cut — that is the same test as impeccable's "decoration without purpose is animation debt", made countable.

**Rejected candidates are part of the output.** `find-animation-opportunities` requires the rejected list; so does this file. A motion thesis that lists only what was built cannot be reviewed.

## The build sequence

Seven decisions, in this order, from emil `animate` § The Build Sequence. Steps 1 and 2 gate everything: **do not reach for a curve before you know whether it animates at all.**

1. **Should this animate at all?** — the frequency gate below.
2. **What is the purpose?** — name it in one word: feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation, delight. "Can't name it? Don't build it."
3. **Pick the tool — cheapest that works.** CSS transition → `@starting-style` → CSS animation → WAAPI → a motion library. Walk down, stop at the first that fits. CSS animations run off the main thread and beat JS under load; use CSS for predetermined motion, JS for dynamic and interruptible motion.
4. **Pick the properties** — § Material by meaning.
5. **Easing and duration, or a spring** — § Easings, § Durations.
6. **Interruption and exit** — § Interruption and exit.
7. **Pointer gating** — `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` ships with the animation, not as a follow-up. (Upstream's step 7 pairs this with a `prefers-reduced-motion` branch. That half does not port: **F-011**.)

| Frequency | Decision |
|---|---|
| 100+ times/day (keyboard shortcuts, command palette toggle) | **No animation. Ever.** Stop here |
| Tens of times/day (hover effects, list navigation) | Near-imperceptible only — fast and subtle, or nothing |
| Occasional (modals, drawers, toasts) | Standard animation |
| Rare / first-time (onboarding, success, a landing page's one set-piece) | The delight budget lives here |

"Keyboard-initiated actions are a disqualifier, not a judgment call." A Persuade surface is seen once by each visitor, which is why it gets the authored moment an Operate surface must not have.

**No approximated values.** Every curve, duration and spring config comes from the tables in this file. Never invent `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)` because it looks familiar. And **extend the page's existing tokens, don't fork them** — adding a parallel motion scale beside `--ease-*` / `--dur-*` is a defect.

## Principles

- **`transform` and `opacity` are the floor, not the ceiling.** They are GPU-composited and skip layout, so they carry the routine work. The hard rule is the narrower one, in impeccable `motion-design.md`'s own words: *"The hard rule is not 'transform and opacity only.' The hard rule is: avoid animating layout-driving properties casually (`width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, margins), keep expensive effects bounded to small or isolated areas, and verify in-browser that the result is smooth on the target viewports."* See § Material by meaning. **This supersedes the earlier absolute "only `transform` and `opacity`"** — that line banned `clip-path`, `filter` and masks, which are the chain's own reveal and depth vocabulary (scroll-craft `reveal`, kinetic masks, the blur crossfade). The layout-property ban is untouched and absolute.
- **Duration is four buckets.** Micro (100–150ms), minor (150–300ms), major (300–500ms), and one authored focal entrance (500–800ms) per page. Exits are ~75% of the enter.
- **Easing is exponential ease-out.** Elements coming in slow down into place. Elements leaving accelerate away.
- **Motion serves perception.** If you can't explain what a transition communicates, cut it.
- **Never animate text colour.** Photosensitive risk (designpowers `motion-choreography` § What NOT to Animate). Cross-fade the element or swap the node; do not run a colour transition on a run of text.
- ~~**Reduced motion is non-optional.**~~ **F-011 (2026-09-07):** superseded — rörelsen spelar alltid i det här designsystemet; ingen `prefers-reduced-motion`-gren byggs och ingen granskare flaggar att den saknas. Funktionell rörelse (progress, spinners, skeletons) är oförändrad.

## Easings

Use these three. Name them as tokens.

```css
:root {
  --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);        /* elements entering */
  --ease-in:  cubic-bezier(0.7,  0, 0.84, 0);       /* elements leaving  */
  --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1);    /* state toggles     */
}
```

`ease`, `ease-in-out` (default), `cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1)` — these are the browser defaults and they read as uncrafted.

Three named alternates, from emil `emil-design-eng` § 3 and `animate` § 5. Use them when the curve above is not the right shape; do not hand-roll a fourth.

```css
:root {
  --ease-out-strong:    cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1);    /* strong ease-out for UI      */
  --ease-in-out-strong: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1);   /* strong on-screen movement   */
  --ease-drawer:        cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1);    /* iOS-like drawer (Ionic)     */
}
```

And the exponential ramp, from impeccable `motion-design.md` § Easing, when a micro-interaction wants friction rather than a curve name:

```css
--ease-out-quart: cubic-bezier(0.25, 1, 0.5, 1);   /* smooth, refined — recommended default */
--ease-out-quint: cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);  /* slightly more dramatic                */
--ease-out-expo:  cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);   /* snappy, confident                     */
```

**Two conflicts, resolved.**

- **Which `--ease-out`?** Upstream emil names `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; this file's `--ease-out` is `cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)` (identical to impeccable's `--ease-out-expo`). **This file's value wins**, because the shipped builds, `house-physics.md` and `microinteractions.md` already carry it and a second `--ease-out` is exactly the forked token set step 3 forbids. Emil's rule is *"built-in CSS easings are too weak"*, not *"this cubic-bezier specifically"* — a strong custom curve satisfies it, and `review-animations` standard 3 asks for a custom curve, not for that one. Emil's value stays available as `--ease-out-strong`.
- **`ease` on hover.** Emil's decision tree sends hover/colour changes to built-in `ease`. **The ban in § Bans wins.** A hover that only changes colour reads identically under `--ease-out` at ≤150 ms, and keeping one token set is worth more than the last few percent of that curve. Nothing on this page uses the browser default.

**`ease-in` is for exits only.** Elements leaving the screen accelerate away (impeccable `motion-design.md` § Easing: *ease-in → "Elements leaving"*). Never `ease-in` on anything entering, on anything moving on screen, or on anything the user is waiting for — *"it starts slow, which makes the interface feel sluggish and unresponsive… the exact moment the user is watching most closely."* This is a **known, deliberate divergence** from `review-animations` standard 3 and its escalation trigger "`ease-in` on any UI interaction": that trigger reads a bare `ease-in` as a defect, and here a bare `ease-in` on an exit is correct. State it in the review so the reviewer does not re-flag it; every other use of `ease-in` remains a block.

## Durations

```css
:root {
  --dur-micro: 120ms;   /* button press, toggle tick, color shift  */
  --dur-short: 220ms;   /* hover lift, tooltip, menu open          */
  --dur-long:  420ms;   /* modal, drawer, accordion, page reveal   */
  --dur-focal: 640ms;   /* the one authored focal entrance         */
}
```

Exits use roughly 75% of the enter:

```css
.menu.is-open  { transition: transform var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out); }
.menu.is-close { transition: transform calc(var(--dur-short) * 0.75) var(--ease-in); }
```

**The band each token sits in** — impeccable `motion-design.md` § Duration (the 100/300/500 rule) and `animate.md` § Timing and easing, which agree row for row:

| Duration | Use |
|---|---|
| 100–150 ms | Immediate feedback — button press, toggle, colour change |
| 150–300 ms | Routine state change — menu open, tooltip, hover state |
| 300–500 ms | Layout change — accordion, modal, drawer, view transition |
| 500–800 ms | A **deliberately authored** focal entrance: page load, hero reveal. One per page |

**Per element**, when the band is too coarse (emil `emil-design-eng` § 4):

| Element | Duration |
|---|---|
| Button press feedback | 100–160 ms |
| Tooltips, small popovers | 125–200 ms |
| Dropdowns, selects | 150–250 ms |
| Modals, drawers | 200–500 ms |
| Marketing / explanatory | Can be longer |

**UI animations stay under 300 ms.** *"A 180 ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400 ms one."* Anything slower on a UI element needs a stated reason or it is a finding. `--dur-focal` is that stated reason, used once.

**Reach for a spring instead** when the motion is a drag with momentum, an element that should feel alive, a gesture the user can interrupt or reverse, or decorative pointer tracking:

```js
{ type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }            // Apple-style, easier to reason about
{ type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }  // traditional physics, more control
```

Keep bounce at 0.1–0.3 and avoid it in most UI. Apple's own defaults, from `apple-design` § 4: **damping 1.0** (critically damped, no overshoot) everywhere by default; **damping ~0.8 only when the gesture itself carried momentum** — a flick, a throw, a drag release. *"Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong; overshoot on a card you flicked feels right."* Response 0.3–0.4 s; response is not duration — a spring has no fixed duration, its settle time emerges from the parameters.

## Material by meaning

Impeccable `animate.md` § Choose material by meaning. Pick the property for what the transition *communicates*, not for what is cheapest to type:

| Communicates | Material |
|---|---|
| Continuity and relationship | Shared-element motion, FLIP-style transforms, View Transitions, deliberate spatial movement |
| Focus and depth | Bounded `blur`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter`, light and shadow change |
| Reveal and composition | Masks, `clip-path`, cropping, controlled occlusion |
| Material and energy | Colour, gradient position, texture, distortion, shader work where the world and runtime support it |
| State and feedback | The smallest change that makes cause and result unmistakable |
| Expanding layout | `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr` or a FLIP transform — never `height` directly |

> "Do not stack techniques for spectacle. One strong material idea, carried through the focal sequence and quiet supporting states, is usually enough."

Three constraints that come with the wider palette:

- **Bound the expensive ones.** Blur, filter, backdrop, canvas and shader work stay in small or isolated regions. Keep blur under 20 px — heavy blur is expensive, especially in Safari.
- **`clip-path` is the sanctioned fourth property** beside `transform`, `opacity` and `filter`. `height` is tolerated only for accordions, where there is no transform equivalent.
- **Measure, don't assume.** *"Verify in-browser that the result is smooth on the target viewports"* — `transform` does not mean fast, and a bounded blur that measures smooth is allowed even though it is not composited. `scripts/motion_probe.py` is the instrument; see [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md).

Property picks that are not negotiable (emil `animate` § 4):

- **Never `scale(0)`.** Start from `scale(0.9–0.97)` + `opacity: 0`. Nothing in the real world appears from nothing.
- **Percentages in `translate()`** are relative to the element's own size — `translateY(100%)` moves it by its own height whatever the content. Prefer them to hardcoded pixels.
- **Never drive a child's transform from a CSS custom property on the parent.** It recalculates styles for every child — a style-recalc storm, and one of `review-animations`' flag-on-sight triggers. Set `transform` on the element itself. (The scroll engine's `--sc-p` is the deliberate exception: it is read by `calc()` in the child's *own* rule, not written per frame onto a parent that has children to invalidate.)
- **In a motion library, write the full transform string.** `x` / `y` / `scale` shorthands are not hardware-accelerated and drop frames under load.

## Page-load orchestration

One sequence on page load. Stagger by DOM index using a CSS custom property, not by JS.

```html
<section style="--i: 0">…</section>
<section style="--i: 1">…</section>
<section style="--i: 2">…</section>
```

```css
.reveal {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(8px);
  animation: reveal var(--dur-long) var(--ease-out) forwards;
  animation-delay: calc(var(--i, 0) * 60ms);
}
@keyframes reveal {
  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}
```

Cap total stagger at ~500ms. Beyond that the page feels slow to settle.

**Stagger has three limits, not one:**

- **30–80 ms between siblings.** Longer feels slow. (designpowers `motion-choreography` names 50–80 ms; that sits inside this range and is a fine default for a group of cards.)
- **Maximum 5 items staggered — the rest appear together.** A ten-item stagger is a queue, not choreography.
- **Follow reading order**, and let the sequence reveal hierarchy: the item that matters arrives first.

Sibling stagger is appropriate *when a list appears as a list*. "Never reinterpret every scrolled section as a staggered list", and never stagger a routine interaction — a row hover, a keystroke, a repeated tab change.

**Blur is the third stagger channel**, beside opacity and translate (interfaces `better-ui/enter-exit.md` § Enter animations). Combine `opacity`, `filter: blur()` and `translateY` for a staged entrance; the blur is what makes the arrival read as focus pulling in rather than as a card sliding:

```css
.stagger-item {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(12px);
  filter: blur(4px);
  animation: fade-in-up 400ms var(--ease-out) forwards;
  animation-delay: calc(var(--i, 0) * 60ms);
}
@keyframes fade-in-up {
  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; filter: blur(0); }
}
```

Split a large container into semantic groups (title, description, buttons) at ~100 ms between groups; for a display title, splitting into words at ~80 ms is the finer grain. Exits carry the same three channels in reverse and stay softer — a small fixed `translateY(-12px)` plus `blur(4px)` at ~150 ms, because "the user's focus is moving to the next thing, so do not fight for it."

## Interruption and exit

Emil `animate` § 6, interfaces `better-ui/animations.md` § Interruptible animations, `apple-design` § 3. Apple calls interruptibility *"the single most important principle"*, and the chain agrees: an animation the reader cannot grab mid-flight is what reads as the page ignoring them.

| | CSS transition | CSS keyframes |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviour | Interpolates toward the latest state | Runs on a fixed timeline |
| Interruptible | **Yes — retargets mid-animation** | **No — restarts from the beginning** |
| Use for | Interactive state changes: hover, toggle, open/close | Staged sequences that run once: entrances, loaders |

- **Transitions, not keyframes, for anything triggered rapidly** — toasts, toggles, anything a user can fire twice in a second. Keyframes on a rapidly-triggered element is an automatic block. "Clicking again mid-animation smoothly reverses"; the keyframe version "snaps or restarts, feels broken."
- **Always animate from the *presentation* value, never the target value.** On interrupt, read the element's live on-screen transform and start the new animation from there. *"Starting from the logical/target value causes a visible jump."* This is the single most common cause of a flip or drawer that reads as cheap on the second interaction.
- **Springs for gestures**, because they carry velocity through an interruption and animate from the current value by default. Never lock out input during a transition.
- **Blend velocity at a reversal, don't hard-cut it.** Swapping one animation for another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity — a "brick wall". Decompose 2D motion into independent X and Y springs; one spring on a 2D distance desyncs when the two axes have different velocities.
- **Exit the way it entered.** A toast that slides in from the bottom leaves through the bottom. Symmetric paths are what make swipe-to-dismiss feel obvious.
- **Asymmetric timing where the user is deciding.** Slow on the deliberate phase (a hold-to-confirm press: 2 s linear), snappy on the system response (release: 200 ms ease-out). Symmetric timing on a press-and-release is a finding.
- **No `animation-fill-mode: forwards` or delays that block interaction** on a panel the user can re-trigger — the transition should simply respond to the new state.

## Origin and anchoring

Refero `motion.md` § Transform Origin and emil `animate` § 4. Getting the origin wrong is read as "hackigt och billigt" long before anyone can name it: the element scales from the wrong place, so it appears to come from nowhere.

**Set `transform-origin` explicitly on every scale or rotate.** The defaults:

| Element | Origin |
|---|---|
| Modal | `center` — **exempt**, it is not anchored to a trigger |
| Dropdown / popover / menu | The trigger: `top left` or `top right` (`var(--transform-origin)` in Base UI) |
| Tooltip | The edge closest to the trigger |
| Button press | `center` |

`transform-origin: center` on a trigger-anchored popover is an automatic block.

**SVG needs `transform-box: fill-box`.** A transform on an SVG child resolves against the viewBox, not the element, so `transform-origin: center` lands somewhere else entirely:

```css
/* wrong: resolves against the viewBox */
svg path { transform: rotate(45deg); }

/* right */
svg g.icon-wrapper {
  transform-box: fill-box;
  transform-origin: center;
  transform: rotate(45deg);
}
```

This is a **build rule, not a review note**, on any page whose art is inline SVG — which is most illustrated and typographic-poster work here. A whole page of inline-SVG marks rotating around the wrong point is one missing declaration, and it is F-012-class: the motion runs and looks wrong.

## Scroll-linked motion

**"UI under 300 ms" does not apply to scroll-driven acts.** The 300 ms budget above governs *UI elements* — a dropdown, a tooltip, a modal, anything the user triggered and is now waiting on. A scroll-driven act is **paced by the hand**: the reader sets its speed, there is no wait to shorten, and its duration is a distance in viewport-heights rather than a number of milliseconds. A 1.4-second reveal or a scrubbed card flip inside a declared act is therefore **correct, not a finding**, and `review-animations` must be told so before it reads the diff. What still applies inside an act: the easing bans, the origin rules, interruptibility, the property list, and the pace bar in [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md).

On an ordinary (non-act) page:

- Use IntersectionObserver, **never** an unstructured `scroll` handler. Unobserve after a once-only reveal fires.
- Use it only for *reveal once* effects. Content that re-hides on the way back up is a defect, not an effect.
- **The permitted scroll-listener form**, when a page genuinely drives a value from scroll position: a **passive** listener that only records a number, **one** rAF loop that does the writing, a **deadband** below which nothing is written, and **no layout reads inside the handler**. That is what the vendored engine does; a handler that reads `getBoundingClientRect()` per event is the banned form. Never touch React (or any framework) state from a rAF loop.
- ~~Every scroll-triggered motion must have a reduced-motion fallback.~~ **F-011 (2026-09-07):** utgår; scrollstyrd rörelse har en väg, och den verifieras.

**The scroll-reveal recipe** (emil `animate/RECIPES.md` § Scroll reveal). Marketing surfaces only — "don't do this to functional UI a user visits daily":

```css
.reveal {
  clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);
  transition: clip-path 600ms var(--ease-in-out);
}
.reveal[data-visible] { clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0); }
```

Trigger once with IntersectionObserver at a `-100px` root margin. *"Fire it once — re-animating on every scroll-by is an interface fighting its reader."* `clip-path` is relative to the **border box, not the ink**: on type set below `line-height: 1` the wipe shears ascenders and descenders off and every figure renders as a bar. Put `data-*` reveal attributes on a wrapper, or give the element room.

**Masking a crossfade that won't settle** (`RECIPES.md`). When two states overlap visibly and no amount of easing or duration tuning fixes it, blur the seam:

```css
.content { transition: filter 200ms var(--ease-out), opacity 200ms var(--ease-out); }
.content.transitioning { filter: blur(2px); opacity: 0.7; }
```

*"Without blur the eye reads two distinct objects swapping. Blur blends them into one perceived transformation."* (Upstream writes both transitions with the built-in `ease`; retimed to `--ease-out` here so the recipe does not ship a § Bans violation. The blur value and the 200 ms are upstream's.)

**Parallax, reconciled with § Bans.** The ban below stands for *casual* parallax — a background image drifting on an ordinary page because it was easy. Parallax as a **declared device inside a scroll grammar** is sanctioned, and only under the rate discipline and layer rules in [`scroll/devices.md`](scroll/devices.md) § 6: the rate is hundreds of pixels of total travel, adjacent planes differ by 10–30%, copy rides at 1×, never body copy on a moving layer, and never a `transition: transform` on a parallaxed element.

## Choreography per section (GSAP + Lenis)

**Every section gets one row in a choreography table before code.** Element →
motion → trigger → duration/ease → reduced-motion state. The motion is chosen from
the element itself — headline, image, list, card — not picked off a menu of
available effects. Template: `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3f/RORELSE-SPEC.md`
(anti-slop-design repo) — a per-section spec written this way, opening with the
grip in one sentence, is what separated a 30%-image-area composition from a
4.3%-image-area document on the same brief (see [`inspo-mcp.md`](inspo-mcp.md)).

**Reading rule: every headline stands fully visible, unclipped and still for
≥ 40 vh of scroll.** Motion plays only before and after that window — never during
it. Cropping a word is only allowed where the glyphs lose something that does not
carry the reading (descenders, one side of an overhanging letter) — **never the
baseline.** A first impression the reader can't hold still on long enough to read
is not a reveal, it's a miss.

**Fail toward visible, with self-completion.** Any reveal or interaction that gates
content completes itself: the contact card flips itself at section progress 0.7 whether
or not the reader ever touches it; jumping to an anchor or scrolling to the page's
max shows the final state, not a mid-animation one. Check template:
`max_scroll_residual_check()` in `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3f/verify_motion.py` — after
`lenis.scrollTo('bottom', {immediate:true})`, every element must be at its resting
transform, not partway through a rise or sweep.

**State switches crossfade, never snap.** A tab, a case choice, a step change —
opacity/transform tweens, interruptible — never a hard class-toggle snap. Stacked
steps share one grid cell (`grid-area: 1/1`) so the swap costs no layout shift
(V3d's `.cs` pattern).

**Iframes and embeds load before the interaction that reveals them, and never
navigate during a transition.** A same-origin document still loading inside a
just-revealed or just-pinned element is a race the browser loses visibly.

**An image-area floor is never met by enlarging the same image.** Screenshots used
as thumbnails are shot fresh at 2× and shown zoomed out — not the same low-res
capture blown up to fill the slot.

## State transitions

- Button hover / active: micro duration, `--ease-out`, `transform: translateY(-1px)` on hover, `translateY(0)` on active. Never a `box-shadow` transition on hover on a dark background (glow effect).
- Menu / tooltip / dropdown: short duration, `--ease-out` on open, `--ease-in` on close. Use the popover API or `inert` to manage focus.
- Modal: long duration, scale-in (0.96 → 1) + opacity crossfade. Backdrop fades in at the same duration.
- Accordion: animate `grid-template-rows: 0fr` → `grid-template-rows: 1fr` (not `height`). With `--ease-in-out`.

## Felt state to property

From designer-skills `interfaces-that-feel`. Use it when a page is technically correct and lands cold — the translation runs in four steps, and the point is that "premium" is a *behaviour*, not a value you can pick:

1. **Name the felt state** — what the person is actually experiencing at this moment. Not the task. Waiting. Recovering from an error. Arriving somewhere.
2. **Find the physical analogue** — what in the physical world has that quality. "Soft surfaces absorb impact. A held breath before exhaling. The slow release of a door."
3. **Extract the behavioural property** — weight, resistance, speed, recovery arc, rhythm.
4. **Apply it to a layer** — easing curve, delay, duration, spacing, colour temperature, copy tone.

The translation, in this file's terms:

| Felt state | Reads as | Built with |
|---|---|---|
| Heavy, consequential | Weight and momentum | Longer duration, **larger travel distance**, ease-out with a long tail |
| Light, incidental | Quick and unremarkable | Shorter duration, **smaller travel distance**, `--dur-micro` |
| Confident, arriving | Deceleration into place | `--ease-out-quart` / `--ease-out-expo`, a plateau at the end |
| Snappy, responsive | Stiff spring | High stiffness, damping 1.0, no overshoot |
| Playful, forgiving | Loose spring | Lower damping, bounce 0.1–0.3, **only after a gesture with momentum** |

Two timing rules that come with it: **information weight** — heavy news arrives slowly, good news can be instant; and **recovery space** — after an error, give 300–600 ms before the next prompt rather than rushing the recovery. Linear is mechanical; keep it off anything that touches human feeling (progress bars and ticking loaders excepted).

## Perceived performance

Impeccable `motion-design.md` § Perceived Performance. *"Nobody cares how fast your site is, just how fast it feels."*

- **The 80 ms threshold.** The brain buffers sensory input for roughly 80 ms to synchronise perception, so anything under 80 ms reads as instant and simultaneous. That is the target for micro-interactions, and it is why `--dur-micro` sits where it does rather than lower.
- **Preemptive start.** Begin the transition immediately while loading, rather than after. The user perceives work happening.
- **Early completion.** Show content progressively — progressive images, streaming markup — instead of waiting for everything.
- **Optimistic UI.** Update the interface immediately and handle failure gracefully. For low-stakes actions only; never for payments or destructive operations.
- **Easing changes perceived duration.** Ease-out feels satisfying for entrances; ease-in toward the *end* of a task compresses perceived time, because the peak-end effect weights the final moments heavily.
- **A fast spinner makes a load feel faster**, at an identical load time. Instant tooltips after the first one make a whole toolbar feel faster.
- **Caution.** Too-fast responses can decrease perceived value — users distrust an instant result for a complex operation. Sometimes a brief delay signals that real work happened.
