commands.description: (foreman) Provides daily practices for reading team energy, shaping culture deliberately, writing unwritten rules, diagnosing accountability gaps, balancing personality types, and building high-performing teams through social connection. Use when a team feels stuck or stale, when collaboration derails despite good intentions, when unwritten norms produce confusion, when new hires struggle to decode the culture, or when a leader suspects the team's vibe is off but cannot articulate why.

commands.name: foreman:thinking-fast-and-slow
commands.description: (foreman) Audits business decisions for cognitive biases using Kahneman's dual-process theory of System 1 (fast, intuitive) and System 2 (slow, analytical) thinking. Covers overconfidence, anchoring, loss aversion, planning fallacy, and availability heuristic. Use when conducting pre-mortems on major initiatives, debiasing fundraising projections, applying reference-class forecasting, sorting decisions by required processing mode, or building structured decision protocols.

commands.name: foreman:thomas-kilmann-conflict
commands.description: (foreman) Diagnoses and resolves conflicts using the Thomas-Kilmann five-mode framework: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, and accommodating, mapped across assertiveness and cooperativeness dimensions. Use when navigating co-founder disagreements, mediating cross-functional team friction, choosing the right conflict mode for high-stakes decisions, expanding personal conflict style range, or designing conflict resolution processes for the organization.

commands.name: foreman:tipping-point
commands.description: (foreman) Analyzes viral growth potential using Gladwell's Tipping Point framework through three rules: the Law of the Few (Connectors, Mavens, Salespeople), the Stickiness Factor, and the Power of Context. Use when product growth is stubbornly linear despite high satisfaction, designing launch strategies for organic adoption, engineering shareable product moments, identifying key influencers in a target market, or diagnosing why a superior product fails to spread.

commands.name: foreman:tone-and-engagement
commands.description: (foreman) Diagnoses and corrects the tonal failures that cause business writing to anaesthetise readers rather than persuade them. Addresses passive voice, nominalizations, hyperformality, sarcasm, and the specific calibration of tone to audience and relationship. Use when drafting client communications, revising documents that feel lifeless or overly formal, preparing sensitive messages that require tonal precision, or building writing standards for a team.

commands.name: foreman:tough-decision-situations
commands.description: (foreman) Addresses the four hardest decision scenarios founders face: teams that cannot reach consensus, choices where every option is bad, decisions that have already gone wrong, and calls that must be made under severe time pressure. Provides structured techniques for each scenario including disagree-and-commit protocols, least-worst analysis, early admission and course-correction frameworks, and recognition-primed decision heuristics. Use when the team is deadlocked and unable to converge, when all available options carry significant downside, when a prior decision has clearly failed and needs triage, when time pressure demands rapid judgment with incomplete information, or when standard decision frameworks assume conditions that do not exist.

commands.name: foreman:trust-equation
commands.description: (foreman) Diagnoses and builds trust using Maister's Trust Equation: Trust = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) / Self-Orientation. Evaluates each variable with evidence-based scoring and prescribes targeted improvements. Use when losing investor confidence, experiencing customer churn despite strong product, repairing damaged stakeholder relationships, preparing fundraising trust strategies, or auditing team trust dynamics.

commands.name: foreman:tuckman-team-stages
commands.description: (foreman) Diagnoses team development stage using Tuckman's five-phase model: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, and Adjourning. Prescribes stage-appropriate leadership actions and identifies progression barriers. Use when a new team is struggling to gel, conflict emerges after initial politeness, teams regress after adding new members, post-acquisition integration stalls, or leaders need to facilitate productive storming rather than suppress it.

commands.name: foreman:understanding-people
commands.description: (foreman) Applies modern personality-decoding and rapid-understanding techniques to entrepreneurial relationships. Covers the Enneagram as a superior alternative to Myers-Briggs for self-awareness and team communication, the discipline of getting anyone even when chemistry is absent, three-question rapid-understanding for first meetings, being interested rather than interesting, and addressing the pervasive loneliness that shapes professional interactions. Use when building cofounder relationships, conducting customer discovery, onboarding new hires, preparing for investor meetings, or diagnosing communication breakdowns within teams.

commands.name: foreman:vuca-framework
commands.description: (foreman) Classifies unpredictable environments into four distinct dimensions -- Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, and Ambiguity -- each requiring a different strategic response: Vision, Understanding, Clarity, and Agility respectively. Use when navigating regulatory grey zones, responding to sudden competitive disruption, reducing operational complexity during scaling, designing rapid experimentation programmes under ambiguity, or building organizational resilience.

commands.name: foreman:wanting-what-matters
commands.description: (foreman) Addresses the meta-question behind all decision-making: whether the entrepreneur is optimising for the right things. Covers the hedonic treadmill and 'happy-when' trap, Dickens's A Christmas Carol as a decision-making parable, what happiness research from the elderly consistently reveals, memento mori as a practical decision filter (the deathbed test), the regret-minimisation framework, and the distinction between ordinary moments and defining moments. Use when a founder suspects they are chasing metrics that do not produce satisfaction, when strategic priorities feel misaligned with personal values, when mortality awareness could sharpen decision-making, or when the question shifts from 'how do I get what I want?' to 'is what I want worth wanting?'

commands.name: foreman:what-is-a-story
commands.description: (foreman) Defines what qualifies as a genuine story versus an anecdote, romp, or report. Teaches the transformation requirement, the Dinner Test, and the personal-narrative principle. Use when a founder's pitch feels flat despite good content, when team presentations list facts without landing emotionally, when someone confuses a sequence of events with a compelling narrative, or when preparing any communication that must move people rather than merely inform them.

commands.name: foreman:win-win-negotiation
commands.description: (foreman) Prepares and conducts negotiations using Fisher and Ury's principled negotiation method from Getting to Yes. Applies four principles: separate people from problems, focus on interests not positions, generate options for mutual gain, and insist on objective criteria. Use when negotiating term sheets, structuring enterprise contracts, resolving co-founder equity disputes, preparing for acquisition discussions, or debriefing completed negotiations for improvement.

commands.name: foreman:writing-effective-emails
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a practical system for writing emails that get read, answered, and acted upon. Covers subject line craft, optimal length, formatting for scanning, tone calibration, CC/BCC etiquette, and when to choose a different medium entirely. Use when composing high-stakes emails to investors or clients, establishing email standards for a team, preparing sensitive written communications, or diagnosing why outreach emails receive poor response rates.

commands.name: foreman:writing-for-navigation
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a structural system for arranging written content so busy readers can find what matters within seconds. Covers BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front), visual hierarchy, headings as signposts, bullet point strategy, formatting discipline, and the map metaphor for document design. Use when structuring investor updates, redesigning internal communications, formatting product announcements, or diagnosing why well-written messages still fail to land.

commands.name: foreman:writing-for-response
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches how to write messages that convert reader understanding into reader action. Covers friction reduction, default design, the power of constrained choices, response-oriented formatting, and the 30-second response test. Use when crafting calls to action in emails or product copy, designing opt-in or enrolment flows, diagnosing low response rates on surveys or meeting requests, or building templates for action-oriented team communications.

commands.name: foreman:writing-memos-and-reports
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a systematic approach to structuring memos, reports, and business letters that inform decisions and drive action. Covers the Issue-Solution-Reason summary framework, the Who-Why-What-When-How planning chart, visual aids, three-audience writing, and business letter conventions. Use when drafting board memos, internal recommendations, market analysis reports, strategic proposals, client-facing letters, or any document longer than an email that must survive scrutiny from multiple readers.

commands.name: foreman:writing-performance-reviews
commands.description: (foreman) Guides the high-stakes process of writing performance appraisals that are specific, fair, legally defensible, and genuinely useful for employee development. Covers the seven evaluation dimensions (attitude, efficiency, human relations, judgment, knowledge, reliability, communication), the spectrum from superb to poor, the discipline of pairing evaluative language with concrete evidence, and the legal implications of imprecise writing. Use when preparing annual or quarterly reviews, designing performance evaluation templates, training first-time managers on review writing, or auditing existing review practices for fairness and consistency.

commands.name: foreman:writing-process
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches the MACJ writing process -- Madman, Architect, Carpenter, Judge -- a four-phase method for producing effective business documents by separating idea generation, organisation, drafting, and editing into distinct sequential tasks. Covers brainstorming, outlining in sets of three, speed writing, and disciplined revision. Use when facing writer's block, struggling to organise complex material, drafting reports or proposals, or when any business document feels overwhelming to start.

commands.name: foreman:writing-with-purpose
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches how purpose and audience analysis determine the form, tone, and content of every business communication. Applies the principle that the same facts, addressed to the same reader, produce radically different letters depending on the writer's objective. Use when drafting any business document, preparing investor updates, writing customer communications, crafting fundraising emails, or any situation where the writer is unsure what tone to strike or how to frame a message.

commands.description: (Sales) Prepare for a sales call with account context, attendee research, and suggested agenda. commands.description: (Sales) Process call notes or a transcript — extract action items, draft follow-up email, generate internal summary. commands.description: (Sales) Research a prospect then draft personalized outreach. Uses web research by default, supercharged with enrichment and CRM. Trigger with "draft outreach to [person/company]", "write cold email to [prospect]", "reach out to [name]".

commands.name: sales:forecast
commands.description: (Sales) Generate a weighted sales forecast with best/likely/worst scenarios, commit vs. upside breakdown, and gap analysis. commands.description: (Sales) Analyze pipeline health — prioritize deals, flag risks, get a weekly action plan. commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: artifact-diagramming
commands.description: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

commands.name: artifact-capabilities
commands.description: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

commands.name: anthropic-skills:learn

# V3g · showcasen blir mjuk · RAPPORT runda 1

Arbetsmapp `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3g`, kopia av V3f. Bara `#showcase`s inre mekanik är
rörd (pin, casebyte, ruta/box, mobilraderna) — komposition, färg, copy och alla andra
sektioner är orörda, per SHOWCASE-SPEC.md.

## Omstart mitt i rundan

Första `Edit`-anropet mot `index.html` nekades av referensgolvet: `Skill(design)` var
avstängd av en kvarglömd testisolering i `.claude/settings.local.json`
(`skillOverrides.design: "off"`, satt för ett tidigare V3f-isoleringstest). Anton tog
bort spärren och sessionen startades om med instruktionen att ladda `Skill(design)` på
nytt och läsa exakt de filer nekningstexten räknade upp. Det gjordes i den ordningen:
`design-catalogue/FEEDBACK.md` (katalogens egen fil, inte `skills/design/references/`-
kopian jag hade läst första gången), `extract/*-design-language.md` för samtliga fyra
valda katalogposter, `references/reference-lock.md`, `references/scroll/devices.md` och
`references/scroll/feel-and-fingerprint.md` i `~/.agents/skills/design/` (den kanoniska
sökvägen nekningen namngav, skild från repots egen `skills/design/`-kopia — innehållet
visade sig identiskt vid jämförelse) samt fingerprint-registret
`wiki/projects/_index/design-fingerprints.md`. Gaten släppte igenom nästa `Edit` utan
ändringar i själva planen — research- och byggarbetet nedan är oförändrat av
omstarten, bara ordningen på läsningen skiljer.

## Kedjan, steg för steg

1. **`Skill(design)`.** Läst i sin helhet (referensgolvets krav gäller varje steg, se
   ovan). TASTE.md och FEEDBACK.md (katalogens fil) lästa. `python
   scripts/catalogue/select.py --brief SHOWCASE-SPEC.md --k 4` gav **deonlibra, tomo,
   example, happyrobot**. Alla fyras `entry.md`, `fold.webp` (som bild) och
   `extract/*-design-language.md` lästa. **Gav inget att låna:** ingen av de fyra
   visar mönstret uppdraget faktiskt behöver (en sticky textruta som crossfadar
   bredvid en scrollande produktvy) — katalogens `select.py` matchar på brief-nyckelord,
   inte på interaktionsmekanik, och det här uppdraget är en smal, låst mekanisk fix,
   inte ett nybygge som behöver en riktningsreferens. Läst för referensgolvets skull,
   ingenting från dem syns i koden. `reference-lock.md`, `scroll/devices.md`,
   `scroll/feel-and-fingerprint.md` och fingerprint-registret lästa (se ovan).
2. **Inspo** (`references/inspo-mcp.md`). En `search_screens("sticky text column that
   crossfades step by step beside a scrolling product view")` → sex träffar, samtliga
   generiska hero-folds (Step, Warby Parker, Design Maestro, basement.studio,
   Superhuman, Tonal) — inspos index är foldautopsier av statiska sidor, ingen av dem
   visar en scroll-driven crossfade-mekanik. En `get_screen("superhuman-com")` för att
   pröva om en fullsida gav mer — samma resultat, bara ännu en hero-fold. **Inget
   lånat.** Mekaniken är fullt specificerad i SHOWCASE-SPEC.md §C och byggd rakt
   därifrån.
3. **Motorskills, i ordning:** `lenis` → `gsap-core` → `gsap-scrolltrigger` →
   `gsap-timeline` → `gsap-performance`. Gav den bindande regeln som faktiskt löste
   grundorsak 3 (`scrub:true`, inte ett numeriskt värde, eftersom Lenis redan är det
   enda utjämningslagret) och regeln bakom grundorsak 1 (en pin skapas en gång, dödas
   aldrig på klick) — båda står redan uttalade i `scroll/devices.md`s "Load-bearing
   rules" och las bekräftade via skillarna innan koden skrevs.
4. **UI-skills.** `ibelick/fixing-motion-performance`: reglerna (aldrig `scrollTop`-
   polling, bara `transform`/`opacity`, mätning innan skrivning) höll redan för filens
   egen `writeCaseScroll`-skriv-om-ändrad-mönster; inget att ändra, bekräftat
   efterlevt. `zeke/swiss-design`: **inte tillämpad.** Skillen bär en egen Tailwind/
   stone-palett, men V3f:s låsta tokens (`--paper`/`--black`/`--grey`/`--mint`/
   `--rust`/`--lacquer`) styr redan sidan och komposition/färg är uttryckligen utanför
   scope den här rundan — att applicera swiss-designs palett hade varit precis den typ
   av kontraktsbrott `design/SKILL.md` Tier 0–2 varnar för (gate 60).

## Grundorsaker — rättade

| # | Orsak (V3f) | Rättning (V3g) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `activateCase` dödade och återskapade pinnen synkront vid klick | Pinnen skapas EN gång i `setupDesktopEngine()`, kallad en gång vid `matchMedia`-init. Ett klick byter bara `activeCaseKey` |
| 2 | Hōrai-iframens `src` sattes först vid klick → navigation under övergången | Båda iframes får sin `src` via `requestIdleCallback` efter `window.load`, långt innan något klick kan hinna ske |
| 3 | Lenis `lerp:0.1` + ScrollTrigger `scrub:0.6` — dubbel utjämning | `scrub:true`. Lenis är det enda utjämningslagret (matchar `scroll/devices.md`s load-bearing-regel, redan uppmätt jank i V3f 2026-09-24) |
| 4 | `caseY` rörde sig 45 % av segmentet, stod still 55 % med en `u*u*(3-2u)`-smoothstep | Ny kurva: 50 %/50 %, `sine.inOut` (`0.5-0.5*cos(π·t)`), noll hastighet i båda ändar |
| 5 | Dragspel: klass-togglad `grid-template-rows:0fr→1fr` per rad | Ersatt av en enda crossfadande ruta (§C): stegen grid-stackade i en cell, en GSAP-tidslinje per case skrubbad av pinnens `onUpdate` |
| 6 | Pinlängden räknades om per case (`n × innerHeight`) → casebyte krävde `refresh()` | Fast längd: `end: () => '+=' + Math.round(6*0.75*innerHeight)`, `invalidateOnRefresh:true`. Calyx' 5 ankare delar samma fasta längd i 5 steg i stället för 6 |

## Bugg hittad och rättad under rundan (utanför grundorsakstabellen)

Efter att grundorsak 1 rättats (pinnen återskapas aldrig) upptäcktes via
`showcase_probe.py` att **den nyvalda casens iframe-scroll aldrig rörde sig** —
`iframe_scroll.max_single_frame_delta_px` låg på exakt `0.0` i varenda körning, både
genom klickfönstret och hela pin-scrollen. Orsak: den kvarvarande `load`-lyssnaren som
fyller `C.y`/`C.w` är villkorad på `activeCaseKey === C.key`, sant bara för Calyx vid
sidladdning. Eftersom båda iframes nu laddas i bakgrunden (grundorsak 2:s fix) hinner
Hōrais `load` avfyras långt innan Hōrai någonsin blir `activeCaseKey`, så villkoret är
alltid falskt och `measureCase(Hōrai)` kördes aldrig — `activateCase` anropade den
heller inte (till skillnad från V3f:s gamla kod, som körde `setupDesktopEngine(C)` per
klick och därmed alltid mätte om). Fix: `activateCase`s desktop-gren anropar nu
`measureCase(C)` explicit vid varje aktivering (billigt, egengated). Bekräftat löst:
`max_single_frame_delta_px` gick från `0.0` till `406–829px` (rör sig korrekt) i
efterföljande körningar, se sheet.png nedan.

## Verifiering (§D)

Server: `serve.py --port 3307 --root .` från repots rot.

### Siffror, V3f-baslinje mot V3g (headless — se miljönot nedan)

| Mätpunkt | V3f baslinje | V3g |
|---|---|---|
| 1440 klick p95 | 33,4 ms | 33,4 ms |
| 1440 genom p95 | 50,3 ms | 33,4 ms (bättre) |
| 1440 störstas scrollY-hopp (klick) | 358,4 px | 281–401 px (två körningar; se not) |
| 1440 max iframe-delta (genom) | 948,8 px | 406–829 px (bättre) |

Spec bad om att mäta och höja 0,45-opaciteten för inaktiva mobilrader om den ger
brödtext under 4,5:1. Räknat för hand och verifierat med ett Python-skript

  runda (sandlådans instabilitet respektive tidsbudget) — se Återstår.

  headless användes som primär mätgrund med motivering ovan.

## Återstår

1. Kör `showcase_probe.py --headed` vid 1440 och 390 på en miljö med fungerande
   GPU/display för en ren headed-mätning efter bugfixen (den här sessionens headed-tal
   är antingen från före fixen eller saknas helt).
2. Kör hela `verify_motion.py`-svepningen (inte bara `showcase_check`) i en stabilare
   miljö — `kontakt_check`, hero-fit m.fl. är overifierade denna runda trots att de
   inte rörts.
3. Bekräfta Calyx' femte ankare (11 px) i en ren körning; om det kvarstår, mät om det
   fanns redan i V3f (ingen sparad baslinjesiffra för just den kontrollen att jämföra
   mot).
4. Full `Skill(a11y-audit)`-körning (skripten + de åtta passen) i stället för bara den
   beräknade kontrastkontrollen ovan.
5. Ingen ny fingerprint-rad behövs (samma grammatik/nav/hero/aktform/close/register
   som V3f, bara `#showcase`s inre mekanik ändrad) — bekräfta det ställningstagandet
   om en framtida runda vidgar scopet utanför showcasen.

Servern (port 3307) stoppad efter rundan.

# V3g · showcasen blir mjuk · RAPPORT runda 1

Arbetsmapp `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3g`, kopia av V3f. Bara `#showcase`s inre mekanik är
rörd (pin, casebyte, ruta/box, mobilraderna) — komposition, färg, copy och alla andra
sektioner är orörda, per SHOWCASE-SPEC.md.

## Omstart mitt i rundan

Första `Edit`-anropet mot `index.html` nekades av referensgolvet: `Skill(design)` var
avstängd av en kvarglömd testisolering i `.claude/settings.local.json`
(`skillOverrides.design: "off"`, satt för ett tidigare V3f-isoleringstest). Anton tog
bort spärren och sessionen startades om med instruktionen att ladda `Skill(design)` på
nytt och läsa exakt de filer nekningstexten räknade upp. Det gjordes i den ordningen:
`design-catalogue/FEEDBACK.md` (katalogens egen fil, inte `skills/design/references/`-
kopian jag hade läst första gången), `extract/*-design-language.md` för samtliga fyra
valda katalogposter, `references/reference-lock.md`, `references/scroll/devices.md` och
`references/scroll/feel-and-fingerprint.md` i `~/.agents/skills/design/` (den kanoniska
sökvägen nekningen namngav, skild från repots egen `skills/design/`-kopia — innehållet
visade sig identiskt vid jämförelse) samt fingerprint-registret
`wiki/projects/_index/design-fingerprints.md`. Gaten släppte igenom nästa `Edit` utan
ändringar i själva planen — research- och byggarbetet nedan är oförändrat av
omstarten, bara ordningen på läsningen skiljer.

## Kedjan, steg för steg

1. **`Skill(design)`.** Läst i sin helhet (referensgolvets krav gäller varje steg, se
   ovan). TASTE.md och FEEDBACK.md (katalogens fil) lästa. `python
   scripts/catalogue/select.py --brief SHOWCASE-SPEC.md --k 4` gav **deonlibra, tomo,
   example, happyrobot**. Alla fyras `entry.md`, `fold.webp` (som bild) och
   `extract/*-design-language.md` lästa. **Gav inget att låna:** ingen av de fyra
   visar mönstret uppdraget faktiskt behöver (en sticky textruta som crossfadar
   bredvid en scrollande produktvy) — katalogens `select.py` matchar på brief-nyckelord,
   inte på interaktionsmekanik, och det här uppdraget är en smal, låst mekanisk fix,
   inte ett nybygge som behöver en riktningsreferens. Läst för referensgolvets skull,
   ingenting från dem syns i koden. `reference-lock.md`, `scroll/devices.md`,
   `scroll/feel-and-fingerprint.md` och fingerprint-registret lästa (se ovan).
2. **Inspo** (`references/inspo-mcp.md`). En `search_screens("sticky text column that
   crossfades step by step beside a scrolling product view")` → sex träffar, samtliga
   generiska hero-folds (Step, Warby Parker, Design Maestro, basement.studio,
   Superhuman, Tonal) — inspos index är foldautopsier av statiska sidor, ingen av dem
   visar en scroll-driven crossfade-mekanik. En `get_screen("superhuman-com")` för att
   pröva om en fullsida gav mer — samma resultat, bara ännu en hero-fold. **Inget
   lånat.** Mekaniken är fullt specificerad i SHOWCASE-SPEC.md §C och byggd rakt
   därifrån.
3. **Motorskills, i ordning:** `lenis` → `gsap-core` → `gsap-scrolltrigger` →
   `gsap-timeline` → `gsap-performance`. Gav den bindande regeln som faktiskt löste
   grundorsak 3 (`scrub:true`, inte ett numeriskt värde, eftersom Lenis redan är det
   enda utjämningslagret) och regeln bakom grundorsak 1 (en pin skapas en gång, dödas
   aldrig på klick) — båda står redan uttalade i `scroll/devices.md`s "Load-bearing
   rules" och las bekräftade via skillarna innan koden skrevs.
4. **UI-skills.** `ibelick/fixing-motion-performance`: reglerna (aldrig `scrollTop`-
   polling, bara `transform`/`opacity`, mätning innan skrivning) höll redan för filens
   egen `writeCaseScroll`-skriv-om-ändrad-mönster; inget att ändra, bekräftat
   efterlevt. `zeke/swiss-design`: **inte tillämpad.** Skillen bär en egen Tailwind/
   stone-palett, men V3f:s låsta tokens (`--paper`/`--black`/`--grey`/`--mint`/
   `--rust`/`--lacquer`) styr redan sidan och komposition/färg är uttryckligen utanför
   scope den här rundan — att applicera swiss-designs palett hade varit precis den typ
   av kontraktsbrott `design/SKILL.md` Tier 0–2 varnar för (gate 60).

## Grundorsaker — rättade

| # | Orsak (V3f) | Rättning (V3g) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `activateCase` dödade och återskapade pinnen synkront vid klick | Pinnen skapas EN gång i `setupDesktopEngine()`, kallad en gång vid `matchMedia`-init. Ett klick byter bara `activeCaseKey` |
| 2 | Hōrai-iframens `src` sattes först vid klick → navigation under övergången | Båda iframes får sin `src` via `requestIdleCallback` efter `window.load`, långt innan något klick kan hinna ske |
| 3 | Lenis `lerp:0.1` + ScrollTrigger `scrub:0.6` — dubbel utjämning | `scrub:true`. Lenis är det enda utjämningslagret (matchar `scroll/devices.md`s load-bearing-regel, redan uppmätt jank i V3f 2026-09-24) |
| 4 | `caseY` rörde sig 45 % av segmentet, stod still 55 % med en `u*u*(3-2u)`-smoothstep | Ny kurva: 50 %/50 %, `sine.inOut` (`0.5-0.5*cos(π·t)`), noll hastighet i båda ändar |
| 5 | Dragspel: klass-togglad `grid-template-rows:0fr→1fr` per rad | Ersatt av en enda crossfadande ruta (§C): stegen grid-stackade i en cell, en GSAP-tidslinje per case skrubbad av pinnens `onUpdate` |
| 6 | Pinlängden räknades om per case (`n × innerHeight`) → casebyte krävde `refresh()` | Fast längd: `end: () => '+=' + Math.round(6*0.75*innerHeight)`, `invalidateOnRefresh:true`. Calyx' 5 ankare delar samma fasta längd i 5 steg i stället för 6 |

Efter att grundorsak 1 rättats (pinnen återskapas aldrig) upptäcktes via
`showcase_probe.py` att **den nyvalda casens iframe-scroll aldrig rörde sig** —
`iframe_scroll.max_single_frame_delta_px` låg på exakt `0.0` i varenda körning, både
genom klickfönstret och hela pin-scrollen. Orsak: den kvarvarande `load`-lyssnaren som
fyller `C.y`/`C.w` är villkorad på `activeCaseKey === C.key`, sant bara för Calyx vid
sidladdning. Eftersom båda iframes nu laddas i bakgrunden (grundorsak 2:s fix) hinner
Hōrais `load` avfyras långt innan Hōrai någonsin blir `activeCaseKey`, så villkoret är
alltid falskt och `measureCase(Hōrai)` kördes aldrig — `activateCase` anropade den
heller inte (till skillnad från V3f:s gamla kod, som körde `setupDesktopEngine(C)` per
klick och därmed alltid mätte om). Fix: `activateCase`s desktop-gren anropar nu
`measureCase(C)` explicit vid varje aktivering (billigt, egengated). Bekräftat löst:

# Accessibility audit

Eight passes over the target, in order. Each pass produces evidence; the report in pass 8 is only as good as what was actually inspected. `references/principles.md` holds the full principle catalog this procedure draws on, tagged by source. `references/report-template.md` holds the exact report skeleton.

**Standing override — F-011 (Anton, 2026-09-07, permanent, global — applies to every audit this skill runs, not just one project):** motion always plays. Do not raise a finding, escalation, or debt-ledger item for an animation, autoplay, or scroll set-piece that ignores `prefers-reduced-motion` or any other browser/OS motion-accessibility signal — that is intentional in every design system this skill audits, not a defect. This is a deliberate, informed trade against real accessibility guidance (vestibular-disorder / motion-sensitivity users lose their opt-out); it is not an oversight, so do not "helpfully" flag it anyway. Every other WCAG check still applies in full, including the hard, preference-independent seizure-safety limit (no content flashing more than three times per second, WCAG 2.3.1) — that one is not a preference, it stays enforced regardless.

## 0 · Scope + coverage

State what you're auditing (URL, files, or a static screenshot set) and what that lets you verify. A static screenshot verifies visual and content findings only — keyboard, screen-reader, and focus-order findings are **inferred, never verified**, and the report must say so.

| Input | Verified | Inferred |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Live URL / running build | Mechanical scripts, keyboard, focus, contrast, reflow, motion | — |
| Static screenshot(s) | Visual contrast (against the pixels shown), content, layout | Keyboard path, screen-reader announcement, focus order, states not shown |
| Source files, no runtime | Semantics in markup, ARIA, labels-in-code | Rendered contrast, computed focus styles, actual tab order |

Never claim coverage you didn't inspect. Say "inferred from static image" or "not verified — no browser" rather than silently upgrading a guess to a finding.

## 1 · Mechanical pass

Run the scripts and read every JSON field before writing findings from them.

```bash
python <S>/scripts/a11y_scan.py <url>     # <S> = this skill's own directory
python <S>/scripts/tab_walk.py <url> [--max 200]
python <S>/scripts/reflow.py <url>
python ~/.agents/skills/design/scripts/contrast.py <url>
python ~/.agents/skills/design/scripts/contrast_over_media.py <url>
```

- **`a11y_scan.py`** — axe-core at desktop (1440×900) and mobile (390×844), merged. Returns `{url, violations: [{id, impact, description, help, viewports, nodes}], passes, incomplete}`. Each violation carries the WCAG tags axe matched it to.
- **`tab_walk.py`** — walks the page with real `Tab` presses. Returns `{stops, issues}` where each issue is `empty_name`, `offscreen`, `order_mismatch`, `no_focus_indicator`, `positive_tabindex`, `focus_trap`, or `unreachable_interactive` (a click handler with no keyboard path).
- **`reflow.py`** — three checks: overflow at 320px width, overflow at 200% zoom emulation, and **unrevealed content**: elements still `opacity: 0` at three scroll depths (a reveal system that never fires). Returns `{overflow320, overflowZoom200, unrevealed, unrevealedSelectors}`. Under F-011 there is no reduced-motion branch left to isolate, so check (c) is read purely as an unrevealed-content count — the AB09 failure where a page shipped empty below the fold.
- **`contrast.py`** / **`contrast_over_media.py`** — rendered-pixel contrast, the second for text over photo or video (worst-case patch, not the mean).

**CARL rule.** Once per project, before trusting a clean pass from any of these five scripts, run them against `~/anti-slop-design/tests/a11y/broken.html` (absolute; the fixture lives in the design-system repo, not in the audited project) (a fixture with a known violation of each kind: missing label, no focus ring, un-reachable click handler, 320px overflow, failing contrast pair) and confirm every script actually reports it. A verifier that passes a broken page is worse than no verifier — it produces false confidence. If that file is missing, say so and create an equivalent fixture before relying on any script's silence as a clean bill. Hash-routed or multi-state pages: run the scripts once per state (`…/index.html#dashboard`, with the modal open) — the scripts only see the DOM they load.

## 2 · POUR pass

Walk Perceivable / Operable / Understandable / Robust. Cite the WCAG 2.2 AA success-criterion number on every finding (`compliance-mapping` tables in `references/principles.md` map design decisions to criteria — use them rather than guessing a number). Cross-reference `a11y_scan.py`'s violations here; each axe rule maps to one or more SC numbers axe already reports.

## 3 · Cognitive pass (COGA)

For each screen or step, rate the three loads — **intrinsic** (inherent to the task, reduce by chunking not by removing function), **extraneous** (added by the design, eliminate ruthlessly), **germane** (the user's actual engagement, protect it by removing the other two). Then check wayfinding's three questions hold at every point: **where am I, where can I go, how do I get back** — each answerable in under a second, without memory. Verify focus (one primary action per screen, interruptions controllable), error recovery (undo, confirmation on destructive actions, preserved input), and memory load (nothing the user must carry in their head between steps that the interface could show instead).

Then rate every screen or step on six dimensions, with the thresholds — this is what turns "feels complex" into a finding:

| Dimension | Low (good) | Medium (review) | High (redesign) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Decisions required | 0–1 | 2–3 | 4+ |
| Items to remember | none | 1–2 | 3+ |
| New concepts to learn | none | 1 | 2+ |
| Steps to complete | 1–2 | 3–5 | 6+ |
| Reading complexity | plain language | some jargon | dense / technical |
| Visual complexity | clean, focused | moderate | cluttered |

**If any single dimension rates High, that screen needs redesign before launch** — the rating is not averaged across the six, exactly as an escalation trigger is never averaged down. Walk the flow as a user who is tired, stressed and unfamiliar; where you pause, re-read, or feel uncertain is a load spike, and the next question is whether the difficulty is intrinsic (chunk it) or extraneous (delete it). Report as a screen-by-screen table with the ratings, then recommendations sorted by impact.

## 4 · Content pass

Reading age 12–14 (grade 6–8; grade 4–6 for buttons, labels, and errors) — flag anything denser. Heading hierarchy: one H1, no skipped levels, headings that alone tell the page's story, and **depth never past H4** — a page reaching H5 has a structure problem, not a markup problem. Labels: every input has a visible, programmatic label; placeholders are never labels. Alt text by the decision table: decorative → `alt=""`; functional → the action; informative → the meaning; complex → short alt plus an extended description nearby; never "image of…". Link text stands alone out of context — no "click here" or "read more". Error messages follow **what happened + why + what to do**, in plain language, never blaming the user. Tables carry a caption and scoped headers, never used for layout. Multimedia: accurate synced captions (never unreviewed auto-captions), transcripts for audio, audio description for meaningful visual content, keyboard-accessible play / pause / stop / volume / seek controls.

**Autoplay — the explicit ruling.** F-011 removes the *preference gate*, not the *control*. Two different things sit under the word "autoplay" and only one of them is overridden:

| Case | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| A silent, decorative video or scroll set-piece that starts on its own and ignores `prefers-reduced-motion` | **Not a finding.** F-011, by design. |
| **Audio** that starts on its own | **Finding, HIGH.** Audio is not motion; it collides with a screen reader and with whatever the person is listening to. WCAG 1.4.2 stands untouched. |
| Any autoplaying media with **no reachable pause / stop control** | **Finding.** The user must be able to stop it once it is running, and that control must be keyboard-reachable and labelled. Removing the preference gate did not remove the user's ability to act. |
| Content flashing more than three times per second | **Finding, HIGH.** Seizure safety, not a preference (WCAG 2.3.1). |

## 5 · Adaptive pass

Respect every system preference automatically, never ask the user to reconfigure what the OS already knows: `prefers-color-scheme` (real dark mode — dark grey not pure black, off-white not pure white), `prefers-contrast`, `prefers-reduced-transparency` (solid surfaces, no backdrop blur), `forced-colors`. `prefers-reduced-motion` is the one preference this skill does not audit — see the F-011 standing override above; everything else in this list is audited in full. Text in `rem`, never `px`; layout survives 200% zoom and reflows at 320px with no horizontal scroll; density has at least a comfortable default and never drops below 44×44 touch targets or 1.5 line-height at any level. Colour independence: every colour-carried meaning has a second encoding (icon, text, pattern, shape), and the interface passes the **greyscale test**. **In running prose, the underline is the accessible indicator and colour is the enhancement** — an inline link distinguished by colour alone fails colour independence no matter how strong the contrast; the design system's own styling clause on this is gate 61, and a link that drops the underline needs a second non-colour channel in its place (weight, a background, a marker), not a stronger hue. Run the greyscale test explicitly — convert the interface to greyscale and confirm status, errors, charts, and links are all still legible — and report the result rather than assuming it.

## 6 · Interaction pass

Native element first, ARIA last — `<button>` for actions, `<a href>` for navigation, never `<div onClick>`; no ARIA beats bad ARIA. Focus-visible ring at least 2px solid with 3:1 contrast against every adjacent colour it crosses, never bare `outline: none`. Hit areas: 24×24 CSS px is the WCAG 2.5.8 AA floor, 44×44 the touch target, 40×40 a reasonable desktop target; extend with a pseudo-element on the label or button, never overlapping another target. Every gesture (swipe, pinch, drag, long-press, shake) has a button-based alternative — gestures are shortcuts, never gatekeepers. Skip link is the first focusable element on any page with repeated navigation. Composite widgets (tabs, menus, toolbars) use roving tabindex — one Tab stop, active item `0`, the rest `-1`, arrow keys move both. Modals set `inert` on the background, trap focus inside, and return it to the trigger on close. **Landmarks: `banner`, `navigation`, `main`, `contentinfo` are the minimum on every page** — screen-reader users navigate by region before they navigate by heading, and a page with no regions is one undifferentiated run. Prefer the native elements (`<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<footer>`) over explicit `role=`; where a landmark type repeats (two navs, several significant forms), each instance carries a distinguishing `aria-label`. **Every `<iframe>` carries a `title`** — an untitled frame announces as "frame" and nothing more, and on a page embedding a map, a video, a preview or a live demo this is the single most likely automated finding. Both checks are cheap and both are routinely missing, because no build reference mentions them; `tab_walk.py` will not catch either, so check the markup. Never a positive `tabindex` anywhere. Paste is never blocked in any field — password managers and 2FA autofill depend on it — and every field about the user carries a meaningful `autocomplete`.

## 7 · Persona walkthrough

Build 4–6 personas spanning permanent, temporary, and situational conditions (not four permanent-disability personas and nothing else — a broken arm and a parent holding a baby belong in the set too). For each persona, walk every key task from the brief and record whether it **works**, **works with friction**, **works with workaround**, or **fails**. Compile into a barrier matrix: task × persona, one cell per combination. A task that fails for any persona is a finding regardless of how it looks for the rest.

**Name the technology, not the disability.** "A blind user" produces a guess; "JAWS on Windows Firefox, navigating by headings" produces a walkthrough. Cover at minimum: one screen-reader user, one keyboard-only user, one low-vision user using magnification, one user with a cognitive difference, and one user in a situational-impairment context.

The inventory to pick from:

| Sense | Technologies, and what each one changes |
| --- | --- |
| Vision | **Screen reader** (JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack) — reads aloud, navigates by headings, links and landmarks. **Magnifier** (ZoomText, OS zoom) — sees only a fraction of the screen at a time. **Braille display** — text to braille in real time, alongside a screen reader. **High-contrast mode** — system-level colour override. |
| Motor | **Switch device** — one or two buttons scanning through options; *much slower than a keyboard, and every extra step counts*. **Voice control** (Dragon, Voice Access) — spoken commands. **Head pointer / eye tracking** — limited precision. **Mouth stick / stylus**. |
| Hearing | Captions, visual alerts replacing audio ones, hearing loop / Bluetooth to hearing aids. |
| Cognitive | **Text-to-speech** (not a screen reader — the person sees the screen but processes better by hearing), reading ruler, simplified view, password managers as memory relief. |

**The switch device is the worst case for anything long and pinned.** A page whose primary content is a several-screen scroll sequence with pinned acts costs a switch user one scan cycle per step, and there is no "skip to the end of the act" unless the build provides one. Walk that case explicitly rather than inferring it from the keyboard walkthrough.

**Scenario template — eight fields**, and a scenario is not done until all eight are filled:

```
Name:            [name]
Role/context:    [who they are beyond their disability]
Technology:      [devices, AT, browser, settings]
Environment:     [where, when, what else is happening]
Task:            [what they are trying to accomplish]
Steps:           [how they interact, step by step, using their AT]
Pain points:     [where the design fails or creates friction]
Success:         [what a good outcome looks like for this person]
```

The scenario's job is to surface a specific failure a developer could fix — not to describe a goal. If it does not name a step where the design breaks, it hasn't been walked.

Two source lists worth pulling from rather than inventing: `situational-impairment-mapping`'s permanent / temporary / situational split per sense (bright sunlight, a noisy train, gloves, one hand holding a child are the same barriers as their permanent counterparts), and `edge-case-identification`'s content cases — long hyphenated names, non-Latin scripts on a Swedish/English page, a single character, an empty value (`references/principles.md` carries both, tagged by source).

## 8 · Report

Assemble in `references/report-template.md`'s exact shape:

- **Coverage table** from Step 0 — what was verified vs. inferred, restated with what actually got inspected.
- **Findings table** — `Severity | Location | Before | After | Why | WCAG | Who`. One row per root cause; list every location a systemic issue reaches. `Who` names the affected persona(s) or user group, not just "users".
- **Escalation triggers** — always `HIGH` the moment confirmed, never averaged down: no accessible name on an interactive control; a keyboard-reachable control with no visible focus indicator; a control reachable by pointer but not keyboard; content flashing more than three times per second (WCAG 2.3.1 — the one motion check that stays, preference-independent); content or a control clipped or unreachable at 320px width or 200% zoom; a contrast pair that fails its required ratio; state or meaning carried by colour alone; a destructive action with no confirmation or undo; truncated content with no way to reach the full value; content reachable only past a scroll edge or disclosure with no visible cue; an error that names no way to recover; a semantic colour used against its meaning.
- **Verdict** — `Block` when any `HIGH` remains, `Approve` otherwise. Never `Approve` coverage you did not inspect.
- **Legal map** — which of EAA/EN 301 549, ADA, Section 508, and WCAG 2.2 AA each finding touches. Most organisations target WCAG 2.2 AA; EAA (in effect since June 2025) and EN 301 549 align with it; ADA and Section 508 case law references it.
- **SEO flag** — mark findings on headings, alt text, `lang`, link text, or reflow as SEO-relevant; the same structural signals search crawlers and screen readers both depend on.
- **Deferred items** append to `.impeccable/a11y-debt.md` in the audited project — never dropped silently. Accepting accessibility debt requires the user's explicit acknowledgement in the conversation, not an assumed sign-off.

### The debt-entry format — an eight-field ADR

A one-line "deferred: contrast on the footer" is how a decision gets silently reversed two redesigns later by someone who wasn't in the room. Write each entry as a decision record (`inclusive/decision-documentation`):

| Field | What goes in it |
| --- | --- |
| **Title** | Clear and searchable — "Form validation: inline errors instead of summary banner", not "form fix". |
| **Date and author** | When, and by whom. |
| **Context** | The situation and the constraints that produced the decision. |
| **Decision** | What was decided, specifically enough to implement. |
| **Alternatives considered** | What else was evaluated and why it was rejected. |
| **Accessibility impact** | Who benefits and how — named groups, not "users". |
| **Risks and tradeoffs** | What was sacrificed, and why that was acceptable. |
| **Evidence** | The testing, research, or WCAG criterion supporting it. |

Plus the four deferral fields this skill requires on top: severity, **who is excluded** (named groups), **severity of exclusion** — blocked or friction — and a **remediation deadline** (critical: this sprint · major: 30 days · minor: 90 days) with a **review date**.

Store it alongside the code where it travels with the implementation. *Never only in someone's head or in a chat thread* — documentation is the immune system that protects a good decision from being undone by someone who doesn't know why it was made.

## Folding a HIGH: mandatory tradeoff analysis

A `HIGH` finding is never quietly downgraded. If one is going to be accepted rather than fixed, it is folded **by name**, through this analysis, and the result goes in the debt ledger in the format above (`inclusive/tradeoff-analysis`). Six questions:

1. **Who benefits from option A?** Which groups gain, roughly how many, and how severe the barrier is without it.
2. **Who benefits from option B?** The same analysis for the alternative.
3. **Who is harmed by each?** Which groups lose access or degrade, how badly, and whether the harm is permanent or temporary.
4. **What is the severity asymmetry?** **Blocked beats friction** — a user who *cannot* complete the task is more severely affected than one for whom it is *harder*, and blockers get removed before friction gets reduced. Permanent conditions outrank situational ones, because a situational user has other options and a permanent user may not.
5. **What is the reversibility?** Reversible → take the faster option and schedule the improvement. Irreversible → take the more inclusive option and accept the delay.
6. **What is the precedent?** A shortcut taken once becomes the standard unless it is documented as an exception.

**Red lines — tradeoffs that are never made:** never ship a feature that is entirely inaccessible by keyboard; never deprioritise a fix that blocks task completion; never treat "we'll fix it later" as acceptable without a tracked item and a date.

**The one crossed red line, and why it does not generalise.** Upstream's fourth red line is *"never remove existing accessibility to meet a deadline"*, and **F-011 crossed it deliberately** — motion-sensitivity users lost an opt-out they previously had. It is exempt not because the rule is wrong but because it was crossed the way this section demands: analysed, named, attested by the decision owner in writing, permanent rather than a deadline expedient, and recorded with its cost stated (`design-catalogue/FEEDBACK.md` F-011). That is the bar. **An attested override is a decision; an unattested one is the red line.** Nothing else in this skill inherits the exemption, and F-011 does not widen by analogy to any other preference.

## Cheapest fix ladder

When more than one fix would work, propose the earliest step that does:

1. **Delete** — the decorative layer eating clicks, the ARIA a native element makes redundant, the ramp nothing needs.
2. **Use the platform** — the native element or control instead of a custom rebuild.
3. **Reuse what the project has** — an existing token, focus style, or spacing step.
4. **Correct the value** — the exact contrast pair, hit-area size, or WCAG-conformant markup.
5. **Add** — a new token, wrapper, or ARIA attribute only the platform truly cannot supply.

A fix proposed at step 5 where step 1 was available is itself a finding.

## Never Approve coverage you did not inspect

If the target was a screenshot, say keyboard and screen-reader findings are inferred. If a script failed to run, say so and mark that check `Not verified` — never let a tool failure silently read as a pass.

## The 30/50/20 testing pyramid

Automated tools (axe, this skill's scripts) catch roughly 30% of real barriers — the mechanical ones. Manual expert testing (tab-through, screen-reader pass, zoom, plain-language read) catches another 50%. The remaining 20% — real-world usability barriers, unexpected workarounds, cognitive and emotional friction — surfaces only in testing with actual disabled users. This skill covers the first two layers rigorously; recommend the third to the user rather than claiming it was done.

## Before you finish

| Mistake | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Claiming a script pass without running it against `tests/a11y/broken.html` first | Run the CARL check once per project before trusting any clean result |
| Reporting a keyboard or screen-reader finding from a static screenshot | Mark it inferred, not verified — say so in the coverage table |
| Averaging an escalation-trigger finding down because the surface is minor | Escalation triggers are `HIGH` on sight, never re-scored |
| A finding with no WCAG criterion cited | Look it up in `compliance-mapping`'s tables before writing the row |
| Silently dropping a Minor finding not in this fix round | Append it to `.impeccable/a11y-debt.md` with severity, owner, and deadline |
| Fixing contrast by changing hue | Change lightness — it's the channel contrast responds to; remeasure after |
| Reporting "not accessible" with no persona named | Name who specifically is blocked and what they were trying to do |
| Treating four personas with the same permanent disability as full persona coverage | Span permanent, temporary, and situational — 4–6 personas, not a single category |
| Proposing a step-5 fix (new ARIA, new token) where step 1–4 would work | Walk the cheapest-fix ladder before proposing an addition |
| A colour-only status indicator passed because the label happened to be nearby | Run the greyscale test explicitly and report the result |
| `Approve` issued on a domain never actually inspected | Mark that domain `Not reviewed` in the coverage table instead |
| An accessibility-debt item deferred with no deadline or owner | Every debt entry needs severity, WCAG criterion, remediation deadline, and explicit user acknowledgement — written in the eight-field ADR shape, not as a one-liner |
| A `HIGH` accepted rather than fixed, with no analysis behind it | Run the six tradeoff questions, name who is excluded and whether they are blocked or merely slowed, and record it with a review date |
| Landmarks and `<iframe title>` never checked because no script reports them | Read the markup: four landmarks minimum, a title on every frame. `a11y_scan.py` catches `region` and `landmark-one-main`; the frame title and the label on a repeated landmark it does not |

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail
commands.description: (ponytail) Forces the laziest solution that actually works, simplest, shortest, most minimal. Channels a senior dev who has seen everything: question whether the task needs to exist at all (YAGNI), reach for the standard library before custom code, native platform features before dependencies, one line before fifty. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra. Use on ANY coding task: writing, adding, refactoring, fixing, reviewing, or designing code, and choosing libraries or dependencies. Also use whenever the user says "ponytail", "be lazy", "lazy mode", "simplest solution", "minimal solution", "yagni", "do less", or "shortest path", or complains about over-engineering, bloat, boilerplate, or unnecessary dependencies. Do NOT use for non-coding requests (general knowledge, prose, translation, summaries, recipes).

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-audit

Use when the user says "audit this codebase", "audit for over-engineering", "what can I delete from this repo", "find bloat", "ponytail-audit", or "/ponytail-audit". One-shot report, does not apply fixes.

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-debt
commands.description: (ponytail) Harvest every `ponytail:` comment in the codebase into a debt ledger, so the deliberate shortcuts and deferrals ponytail leaves behind get tracked instead of rotting into "later means never". Use when the user says "ponytail debt", "/ponytail-debt", "what did ponytail defer", "list the shortcuts", "ponytail ledger", or "what did we mark to do later". One-shot report, changes nothing.

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-gain

commands.name: ponytail:ponytail-review

commands.name: foreman:ai-augmentation-not-automation
commands.description: (foreman) Makes the strategic and moral case for AI augmentation over pure automation, providing leaders with frameworks for job redesign, creativity-driven AI deployment, and long-term workforce investment. Draws on the centaur model from chess and case studies across industries to demonstrate that human-AI collaboration outperforms either alone. Use when deciding between automating jobs and redesigning them, when AI adoption is eroding workforce skills, when boards pressure for automation-driven cost cuts, when designing new roles that pair human creativity with AI capabilities, or when facing the long-term consequences of over-automation.

commands.name: foreman:ai-communication-culture
commands.description: (foreman) Equips leaders to build flat, participative communication cultures that enable successful AI adoption by bridging technical and business teams, democratising data, and establishing feedback loops. Covers the symphony conductor model, soliciting expert feedback, removing bureaucratic obstacles, and building shared responsibility. Use when AI projects fail due to communication breakdowns, when data scientists and business leaders operate in silos, when employees lack channels to provide AI feedback, when hierarchical structures block information flow, or when leaders need to translate between technical and business perspectives.

commands.name: foreman:ai-emotional-intelligence
commands.description: (foreman) Argues that emotional intelligence becomes strategically critical precisely because of AI -- not despite it -- and provides leaders with practices for developing the soft skills that constitute the human competitive advantage in an AI-saturated economy. Covers empathy, self-awareness, communication beyond technical details, curiosity, proactive problem-solving, trust-building through vulnerability, and coaching teams in EI. Use when an AI project is failing due to poor leadership connection, when technical leaders cannot engage the workforce emotionally, when employees feel reduced to data points, when building the case for soft skills investment alongside AI investment, or when developing the human capabilities that AI cannot replicate.

commands.name: foreman:ai-era-leadership
commands.description: (foreman) Prepares leaders for daily effectiveness in an AI-augmented workplace by focusing on the human capabilities that machines cannot replicate. Covers five irreplaceable leadership skills (interpersonal intelligence, analog relationship-building, creative unpredictability, domain credibility, and preskilling), practical routines for leading hybrid human-AI teams, and strategies for staying relevant as automation reshapes every function. Use when planning workforce development around AI adoption, when leaders feel threatened by automation, when building AI-human collaboration norms, or when advising on career resilience in technology-disrupted industries.

commands.name: foreman:ai-human-centered-approach
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a comprehensive framework for deploying AI in ways that respect employee psychology, preserve human agency, and treat workforce well-being as a strategic priority rather than an afterthought. Addresses the hidden fears employees harbour about AI, the psychological damage of algorithmic supervision, and the practical steps for making human needs central to technology decisions. Use when employees resist AI adoption, when algorithmic monitoring is eroding morale, when AI-driven productivity targets create burnout, when planning an AI rollout that affects frontline workers, or when an AI project is failing and the technology is not the problem.

commands.name: foreman:ai-inclusive-collaboration
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a comprehensive framework for designing inclusive human-AI collaboration that keeps all stakeholders at the design table. Addresses exclusion dynamics, algorithm aversion, trust deficits, silo formation, and the human cost of automation-first strategies. Use when employees resist AI adoption, when AI design excludes non-technical voices, when human-AI collaboration feels extractive rather than empowering, when organisational silos hinder AI scaling, or when leaders need to reward human contributions in AI-augmented work.

commands.name: foreman:ai-learning-for-leaders
commands.description: (foreman) Guides non-technical leaders through building AI savviness without becoming AI experts, closing the gap between AI understanding and AI deployment. Applies the 'just savvy enough' principle and lifelong AI learning framework. Use when a leader feels inadequate about AI knowledge, defers too heavily to technologists, needs to build a business case for AI, wants to lead AI adoption without a technical background, or seeks to distinguish AI-knowledgeable from AI-savvy leadership.

commands.name: foreman:ai-purpose-driven-questions
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches leaders to ground AI adoption in organisational purpose by asking the right questions before selecting tools. Applies the purpose-driven framework to prevent technology-for-technology's-sake deployments. Use when evaluating AI investments against business goals, when data scientists operate without strategic direction, when AI projects lack clear problem definitions, when aligning AI initiatives with company values, or when leaders are tempted to adopt AI because competitors have.

commands.name: foreman:ai-stakeholder-balance
commands.description: (foreman) Guides leaders through the ethical and strategic complexities of balancing multiple stakeholder interests during AI adoption, from employees and customers to society at large. Provides frameworks for responsible AI deployment, stakeholder impact mapping, and moral decision-making when efficiency gains conflict with human welfare. Use when evaluating whether an AI deployment will harm employees or customers, weighing automation against workforce impact, facing pressure to prioritise shareholders over other stakeholders, designing an AI ethics governance structure, or confronting the societal consequences of algorithmic decision-making.

commands.name: foreman:ai-vision-and-strategy
commands.description: (foreman) Guides leaders in developing and communicating a compelling AI vision that inspires rather than threatens, choosing augmentation over replacement as the strategic paradigm. Covers Perspective 1 (AI replaces humans) vs. Perspective 2 (AI augments humans), the tech-driving-tech trap, holistic communication, ethical foresight, and agile visionary leadership. Use when setting long-term AI strategy, when employees fear AI will eliminate their jobs, when AI adoption lacks a unifying narrative, when vision statements betray organisational identity, or when leaders need to translate AI potential into a story that builds commitment.

commands.name: foreman:ambidexterity
commands.description: (foreman) Applies O'Reilly and Tushman's organizational ambidexterity framework to balance exploitation of existing business with exploration of new opportunities. Assesses resource allocation between core operations and innovation initiatives, designs structurally or contextually ambidextrous organizations, and evaluates innovation portfolios. Use when a company needs to protect its core revenue while pursuing new growth, launching separate innovation units, or diagnosing why exploratory initiatives are being starved by day-to-day operations.

commands.name: foreman:appreciative-inquiry
commands.description: (foreman) Guides strengths-based organizational change using Cooperrider's Appreciative Inquiry 4D cycle: Discovery, Dream, Design, and Delivery. Surfaces peak experiences and positive patterns to amplify what works rather than fixing what is broken. Use when addressing team morale, redesigning processes, integrating acquisitions, reframing organizational challenges, or running culture transformation initiatives where traditional deficit-based problem-solving has stalled.

commands.name: foreman:art-of-war
commands.description: (foreman) Applies Sun Tzu's strategic principles to competitive business situations, covering self-knowledge and competitor intelligence, winning without direct confrontation, speed and timing, terrain analysis, and strategic positioning. Use when assessing competitive landscapes, developing market entry strategies, evaluating when to fight or avoid competitors, conducting competitive intelligence audits, or designing stealth positioning for startups facing well-resourced incumbents.

commands.name: foreman:balanced-scorecard
commands.description: (foreman) Builds and evaluates Kaplan and Norton's Balanced Scorecard across four perspectives: Financial, Customer, Internal Process, and Learning and Growth. Creates strategy maps linking causal chains from learning investments through process improvements to customer outcomes and financial results. Use when designing KPI systems, aligning teams around strategy, diagnosing why financial metrics are lagging, auditing measurement balance, or establishing leading indicators for organizational health.

commands.name: foreman:belbin-team-roles
commands.description: (foreman) Analyzes team composition using Belbin's nine team roles across Thinking, Action, and People categories. Maps team members to roles such as Plant, Shaper, Coordinator, Implementer, and others to identify gaps, overlaps, and imbalances. Use when hiring to fill role gaps, diagnosing recurring team conflicts, auditing founding team balance, resolving execution problems caused by missing behavioral profiles, or assessing board composition.

commands.name: foreman:black-swans
commands.description: (foreman) Applies Taleb's Black Swan theory to assess and mitigate exposure to rare, high-impact unpredictable events. Distinguishes between Mediocristan and Extremistan domains, designs barbell strategies, builds antifragility, and audits business vulnerabilities including supply chain concentration, customer dependency, and regulatory risk. Use when stress-testing a business model, evaluating tail risks, designing resilience architecture, or building robust strategies that survive shocks rather than attempting to predict them.

commands.name: foreman:blue-ocean-strategy
commands.description: (foreman) Applies Kim and Mauborgne's Blue Ocean Strategy to create uncontested market space through value innovation. Uses the Strategy Canvas to map competitive factors, the ERRC Grid to Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create value elements, and the Three Tiers of Noncustomers to identify untapped demand. Use when entering saturated markets, escaping price-based competition, redesigning a value proposition, identifying noncustomer segments, or evaluating whether a new venture creates a genuinely new market category.

commands.name: foreman:building-story-stakes
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches five named techniques for creating and sustaining narrative tension in any story. Applies when a founder needs to hold an audience's attention through a pitch, investor update, all-hands talk, or customer case study. Use when a narrative feels flat, when attention wanders mid-presentation, or when the storyteller senses the audience could walk away without consequence.

commands.name: foreman:building-thinking-strength
commands.description: (foreman) Develops the four internal muscles required for clear thinking -- self-accountability, self-knowledge, self-control, and self-confidence -- using the Clear Thinking strength-building system. Covers setting personal standards above external requirements, choosing exemplars, building a personal board of directors, and practising in sandboxes. Use when blaming external factors for poor outcomes, struggling to say no under social pressure, lacking the confidence to execute a difficult decision, noticing that team standards have drifted toward mediocrity, or seeking a structured approach to personal operating system design.

commands.name: foreman:business-model-canvas
commands.description: (foreman) Structures and evaluates business models using Osterwalder's nine-block Business Model Canvas: Customer Segments, Value Propositions, Channels, Customer Relationships, Revenue Streams, Key Resources, Key Activities, Key Partnerships, and Cost Structure. Use when designing a new venture, comparing business model alternatives, stress-testing assumptions, planning pivots, exploring revenue model options, or identifying hidden dependencies between business model components.

commands.name: foreman:business-writing-for-leaders
commands.description: (foreman) Sharpens leadership writing through four principles: write for the reader, lead with clarity, keep it simple, and sound human. Use when drafting company-wide announcements, writing investor updates, composing emails that require action, editing team communications for clarity, or noticing that written messages consistently generate confusion or non-response.

commands.name: foreman:career-strategy-for-leaders
commands.description: (foreman) Guides leaders through deliberate career design -- calculating timelines, auditing career fuel, breaking career-limiting habits, avoiding success traps, and aligning trade-offs with evolving values. Use when a leader feels stuck, faces a career crossroads, suspects their success has become a cage, needs to break a recurring bad habit, or wants to shift from reactive career drift to intentional career architecture.

commands.name: foreman:carnegie-win-friends
commands.description: (foreman) Applies Dale Carnegie's interpersonal influence principles for building relationships, earning trust, and leading without authority. Covers techniques for handling people, making others feel valued, winning people to your thinking, and changing behavior without giving offense. Use when building advisory networks, repairing strained stakeholder relationships, improving investor communications, navigating co-founder conflicts, or developing the interpersonal skills that underpin hiring, sales, and fundraising.

commands.name: foreman:choosing-and-executing
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a toolkit for moving from deliberation to commitment and from commitment to results. Covers the cost of decision paralysis, the 70% rule for when to stop gathering information, implementation planning after the choice is made, transparency as a trust mechanism, handling challenges to decisions, and combating second-guessing through process review rather than outcome regret. Use when stuck in analysis paralysis, when a decision has been made but needs implementation momentum, when stakeholders challenge or resist a decision, when second-guessing erodes confidence, or when building a decision communication plan.

commands.name: foreman:cialdini-influence
commands.description: (foreman) Applies Cialdini's seven principles of ethical persuasion -- Reciprocity, Commitment and Consistency, Social Proof, Authority, Liking, Scarcity, and Unity -- to business contexts including sales, marketing, fundraising, and negotiation. Use when designing conversion funnels, optimizing sales processes, preparing fundraising strategies, auditing marketing materials for persuasive effectiveness, planning negotiation tactics, or building community-driven growth while maintaining ethical boundaries.

commands.name: foreman:clarity-and-concision
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches techniques for achieving relentless clarity and ruthless concision in business writing, including the 20-word sentence rule, concrete detail over abstraction, word economy tactics, and the reader's perspective test. Features extensive before/after examples demonstrating how bloated corporate prose can be cut by 50-70% without losing meaning. Use when tightening any business document, eliminating wordiness, improving readability scores, preparing executive summaries, or when writing feels vague or overlong.

commands.name: foreman:coalition-and-partnership-games
commands.description: (foreman) Analyses partnership structures, cofounder equity splits, and alliance formation using coalitional game theory. Applies Shapley Value for contribution-based allocation, imputation sets and the core for stability testing, and coalition disintegration models to predict breakups. Use when splitting equity among cofounders, structuring joint ventures, negotiating alliance terms, evaluating vendor partnerships, diagnosing why a partnership is failing, or determining fair cost-sharing among unequal participants.

commands.name: foreman:competitive-negotiation
commands.description: (foreman) Executes the competitive negotiation process from opening move through final concession: anchoring strategy, ambitious asking, concession architecture, midpoint management, impasse-breaking through linkage, and closing discipline. Provides actionable protocols for value-claiming negotiations. Use when setting price in a sales negotiation, responding to an aggressive counter-offer, planning concession sequences for fundraising, structuring opening bids in acquisition talks, countering procurement hardball in enterprise deals, or coaching a sales team to stop discounting reflexively.

commands.name: foreman:connecting-with-people
commands.description: (foreman) Applies advanced interpersonal techniques for building genuine, lasting connections in entrepreneurial contexts. Covers the power of validation as the deepest form of listening, leading with 'How can I help you?' as a first-meeting strategy, maintaining authentic online identity, vulnerability as a professional strength, and the Platinum Rule that supersedes the Golden Rule by treating others as they want to be treated. Use when building investor relationships, resolving cofounder conflicts, designing customer-experience strategy, navigating cultural differences in international partnerships, or cultivating the authentic personal brand that underlies fundraising, hiring, and sales.

commands.name: foreman:cooperative-negotiation
commands.description: (foreman) Guides the practitioner through cooperative negotiation execution: transitioning from positions to interests, deploying empathy strategically, and following a structured six-step roadmap to resolution. Use when a competitive stance has stalled, when the relationship matters as much as the deal, when negotiating with a more powerful counterparty, when seeking creative value that positional bargaining cannot unlock, or when preparing for partnership, licensing, or joint-venture conversations.

commands.name: foreman:covey-seven-habits
commands.description: (foreman) Applies Stephen Covey's Seven Habits framework for personal and interpersonal effectiveness, progressing from dependence through independence to interdependence. Covers proactivity, mission clarity, prioritization, Win/Win thinking, empathic listening, synergy, and renewal. Use when conducting personal effectiveness audits, drafting mission statements, preparing Win/Win negotiations, resolving co-founder conflicts, designing founder renewal plans to prevent burnout, or building character-based leadership culture.

commands.name: foreman:creative-collaboration-and-context
commands.description: (foreman) Explores how creative collaboration produces outcomes neither party could achieve alone, covering reference points without copying, the role of creative mythology, the prism of self as competitive advantage, context as meaning-maker, cross-domain adaptation, and translation as a creative act. Use when building creative partnerships, navigating co-founder dynamics, assembling creative teams, repositioning a product through context change, adapting business models across industries, translating technical innovation for new markets, or understanding why the same idea succeeds in one context and fails in another.

commands.name: foreman:creative-completion-and-renewal
commands.description: (foreman) Addresses the hardest creative act -- finishing and releasing work -- covering the tension between experimenter and finisher mindsets, making choices when everything feels possible, accepting shades rather than absolutes, ending projects to begin anew, approaching new work with a clean slate, knowing when to stop refining, and recognising the energy living inside completed work. Use when struggling to ship a product, paralysed by perfectionism, unable to choose between competing directions, managing the transition between projects, deciding when a product version is ready for release, or recovering creative momentum after a major launch.

commands.name: foreman:creative-flow-and-inspiration
